So the form is a smooth tapered spear that becomes dead parallel-sided for its bottom quarter and is chopped flat at the soil line. Plant height ~210px against a max width of 48px, an aspect near 4.4:1 tall-narrow, on a species whose packet aspect is 1. Max width is 11% of frame. Surface is uniform mid-green (sampled RGB 36,73,56) with soft vertical light/dark rib striping running the full length. ON THE MUST-READS, all three fail: (1) 'hugely swollen bulbous grey caudex base' - entirely absent, confirmed at 4x zoom. The bottom of the plant is a straight-flanked green column of constant 48px; there is no swelling, no flare, no shoulder, and no neck-in above a fat trunk, and there is no grey pixel anywhere in the asset - the entire plant is one green. An Adenium caudex should balloon to roughly 35-50% of frame width and then pinch sharply inward; this is 11% and parallel. (2) 'few thick stubby branches' - absent, zero branching, a single continuous axis from soil to flower. (3) 'bare stems with leaves and flowers only at the ends' - the stem is bare, but there is no leaf geometry anywhere on the asset; the apex runs straight from smooth green stem into the flower with no glossy dark spoon-shaped tuft, so the read is 'leafless cactus', not 'bare branch tipped with a leaf rosette'. CORRECTIONS TO THE ORIGINAL CLAIM, which is substantially right but imprecise in three places: (a) it is not really a saguaro/organ-pipe silhouette - a saguaro is parallel-sided its whole length and blunt-topped, whereas this tapers continuously to a 14px point, so it reads closer to a young smooth cereus or an asparagus/agave spear; the ribbing cue is genuinely there and is itself wrong for Adenium, whose trunk is smooth. (b) The claim says 'one flat pink daisy' - confirmed at 5x: exactly one terminal bloom, 12 rounded pink petals radiating face-on around a disc. But the disc is DARK OLIVE-BROWN, noticeably darker than the petals, which is the precise inverse of the required 'pale throat' - so the flower is not merely 'not pale-throated', it is actively contrast-reversed. It is also singular and terminal where the packet calls for flowers CLUSTERED at the tips, so count and placement both fail alongside shape. (c) 'green column' undersells that the flower is the only non-green element in the whole image; there is no second colour mass to carry the grey trunk read even partially. VERDICT: this reads as the wrong organism - a flowering columnar cactus - and the one must-read the packet note calls 'the whole point' (the fat bottle-shaped trunk) is not present in any size or location. FAIL stands. The fix is a full re-silhouette: a squat wide grey-tan bottle caudex occupying the bottom ~45% of the frame and ~40% of frame width, pinching into two or three short thick bare limbs, each ending in a small tuft of dark glossy spoon leaves plus a cluster of pink trumpets seen partly in three-quarter view with pale centres.

rows.readsAs: a pale green succulent rosette or a closed lotus flower, with a sunflower floating in the sky above it
rows.defect: The render is broken - the small yellow flower is stranded in empty space roughly a third of the frame ABOVE the plant, touching nothing, at the height where the sibling rosettes put their stalk-tip beads, so it reads as a detached artefact. Beyond that the plant is not a prickly pear: the pads all radiate from one ground point in the family fan arrangement instead of being stacked end to end off each other, and it is completely smooth - no areoles, no glochid tufts, no long spines anywhere on any pad (only two or three stray hairline scratches), and no magenta tunas ringing the top pad rims. A stranger names this a fat-leaved succulent, not an Opuntia.
rows.fix: Reattach or delete the floating flower, restack the pads as two or three flat ovals joined edge-to-edge in a jointed chain, then cover every pad face with a regular grid of areoles carrying spine tufts and ring the upper pad rims with upright barrel-shaped magenta fruits.
rows.verifyWhy:
FAIL upheld — all three mustReads are absent — but two details of the claim need correcting before anyone fixes against it.

WHAT I SAW (440x440; pixel-scanned and re-rendered at 3x, 6x and 8x).

SILHOUETTE / BODY: five to six pale oval blades, each a smooth unbroken ellipse, all fanning outward from a single point on the ground line and overlapping like a hand of cards. Ink bbox x107-332, y84-322. There is no joint, no waist, no necking, and no second-generation pad growing off the edge of a first — nothing is chained end to end. Read is a lotus/water-lily bud or a fat-leaved Echeveria-type rosette. The judge's 'oval pads all radiating from one ground point instead of a jointed end-to-end pad chain' is exactly right and is the single biggest defect: an Opuntia's identity IS the pad-off-pad chain, and the drawing has a rosette generator underneath it.

AREOLES/GLOCHIDS/SPINES: confirmed absent. At 6x on the outer rim of the right pad and the top rim of the rear pads, every silhouette edge is a clean anti-aliased curve — zero spine projections, zero notches, zero tufts, not even a 1px stub. CORRECTION TO THE CLAIM: the judge said 'zero areoles' and then said nothing about what IS on the pad faces. There is surface detail, and it is worse than nothing — each blade carries two or three thin dark strokes drawn as a vertical midrib with short lateral branches meeting it at an angle (visible on every pad; clearest on the right pad at ~x255-300, y230-290). Those read unambiguously as LEAF VENATION, which actively drags the organism toward 'broadleaf succulent leaf' and away from 'cactus cladode'. The fix is not just to add areoles, it is to delete the vein strokes and replace them with a scattered grid of small dark areole dots each carrying a glochid tuft plus paired long spines that break the silhouette edge.

MAGENTA TUNAS: confirmed absent by pixel count, not by eye — a full-frame scan for magenta (r>100, b>80, g<0.7r) returns exactly 0 pixels in the entire image. Nothing sits on any pad rim; the top rims are bare smooth arcs.

COLOUR: an additional miss the judge did not state. The pad fill is a warm yellow-green (dominant buckets rgb(152,184,136), rgb(168,200,152), rgb(184,216,152) — g>r>b). The packet calls for blue-grey green. The hue needs to go cooler and duller, toward a glaucous blue-grey.

THE FLOATING FLOWER — CLAIM PARTLY WRONG ON SCALE. The detachment is real: the yellow object occupies y85-114, x206-234 (a ~29x30px 11-petal daisy with a darker disc), and the plant's first ink row is y151 (faint edge) / y165 (solid), so there is a band of pure background between them and it touches nothing. But it is NOT 'a third of the frame above the plant' — the gap is 37-50px on a 440px frame, roughly 9-11% of frame height, and the flower centre sits at ~23% down the frame. Anyone hunting a one-third offset will look in the wrong place. TWO further points the judge missed: (a) the flower is anchored to nothing at all, so this is a detached-decoration bug in the harvest placement, not merely a bad offset; (b) the packet's harvest is 'barrel-shaped magenta fruits sitting upright on the rim of the top pads' — a yellow daisy is the wrong harvest object entirely, so relocating it onto the plant would still not satisfy the row. It should be replaced with upright magenta barrel tunas seated on the top pad rims.

VERDICT: flat overlapping paddle chain — absent (rosette instead). Areoles with glochids and spines — absent (leaf veins instead). Magenta tunas — absent (0 magenta pixels). Three of three mustReads missing and the organism reads as the wrong plant. FAIL.

rows.readsAs: a yucca or agave rosette with a thin flower stem
rows.defect: The narrowest blades in the batch make this the closest read of the five, but it is still the shared fan chassis, and its own two distinguishing must-reads are missing or too weak. There are no curly white fibres peeling anywhere along the leaf edges - every margin is clean - and the promised tall panicle of waxy cream bells is only five tiny white ovals clustered in a two-centimetre knot at the very top of an otherwise bare hairline stalk, so it reads as a bud or a berry rather than a hanging flower panicle. The blades also carry the same herringbone venation as the Agave, which a stiff sword leaf should not show.
rows.fix: Hang loose curling white threads off both edges of most blades, and expand the top of the stalk into a broad branched panicle of dozens of nodding cream bell flowers so the harvest reads at thumbnail size.

rows.readsAs: a cluster of green-and-red ice-cream cones, or Sarracenia if you already know Sarracenia
rows.defect: The third must-read is simply absent: the pitcher throat has no red vein network. Zoomed in, the tube carries a few flat vertical dark-olive ribs that read as celery/bamboo ridging, the mouth is a single clean pink outline ring, and the interior is a uniform flat dark brown with no netting, no reticulation, no crimson at all. The pitchers also taper to a sharp POINT at the bottom and float on those points — nothing meets the ground, there is no basal rosette or soil, so the cones read as standing on their tips like traffic cones inverted. The hood is one flat solid leaf-blade with no underside, no vein and no attachment, so it reads as pasted on rather than as a continuation of the pitcher.
rows.fix: Draw the red vein reticulation — an anastomosing crimson net over the upper third of each tube and across the hood's inner face and the peristome — and flatten the pitcher bases into a ground-level cluster so the tubes rise out of a rosette instead of balancing on points.

rows.readsAs: an orange pinwheel or a spoke diagram with white beads on the rim; a sea anemone at thumbnail size
rows.defect: The tentacle-plus-droplet must-read is present but confined to the wrong place: the glandular hairs only fringe the OUTER rim of each paddle, and the entire paddle face is bare flat orange. Real Drosera is furred with tentacles across the whole blade, and that furred surface is what makes the plant legible. The colour is also wrong on the reference's own terms — leafColour calls for green flushed crimson, and there is not one green pixel anywhere; every leaf, every petiole and the hub are the same single orange-red. The scorpioid flower stalk is entirely missing. Composition is a perfectly symmetric radial spoke wheel converging on a single hard point, drawn dead top-down, which reads as a logo or a wiring diagram rather than a low rosette, and the droplets render as opaque white pearls with no transparency or highlight, so they read as popcorn rather than glue.
rows.fix: Cover the whole paddle surface with tentacles, not just the margin, and make the drops translucent with a specular dot; give the petioles green with a crimson flush and tilt the rosette off dead-top-down so it sits on ground rather than reading as a wheel.

rows.readsAs: red rambutan or spiky strawberries on green stalks — a bunch of bristly fruit, not a trap
rows.defect: The identity must-read is absent. At 4x there is no clamshell anywhere in the image: every trap is a single solid red BALL with a green collar, with no midrib, no hinge, no seam, no two lobes and no gape. The teeth do not interlock along a closing edge — they radiate outward from the whole circumference like a sunburst, which is a burr, not a fringe. Because the trap is a closed sphere and its exterior is red, the red glandular INTERIOR must-read cannot be present either; the red is on the outside, which inverts the plant. The third must-read fails too: there is no low ground rosette and no flat winged petioles, only narrow uniform green rods converging to a point, so the whole thing reads as a picked bouquet floating above its shadow. The two central traps also overlap into one undifferentiated red mass, losing even the count.
rows.fix: Rebuild the trap as two hinged lobes seen from the side, open at 45 degrees on a visible midrib hinge, green outside with the crimson glandular surface only on the inner faces, and put the marginal teeth as interlocking cilia along the two lip edges only; broaden the petioles into flat leaf-like wings lying in a ground rosette.

rows.readsAs: an ornamental fountain grass or a small pampas clump with a seed bristle
rows.defect: The identity of a cattail is the fat brown velvet SAUSAGE, and it is not here — the brown spike is a thread barely wider than a leaf blade, and it has no separate thin male spike above it. The leaves also splay outward almost to horizontal in a fountain instead of rising as straight vertical straps, and no bare round stem is visible because the stem is buried inside the leaf spray. This is the same fountain drawing as Papyrus and Wild Rice, recoloured.
rows.fix: Draw the spike as a genuinely thick brown cigar — roughly one-sixth as wide as it is tall, blunt at both ends — carried on a clean bare stem that stands clear ABOVE the leaves, with a thin pale bristle continuing above it; and straighten the strap leaves to rise near-vertically from the waterline.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, with two of the stated causes corrected. Measured on the 440x440 PNG (background sampled at 5,6,12).

WHAT IS THERE. A single fountain of ~14 pale grey-green strap blades springing from one point at the base, plus one thin vertical stalk carrying a small tan spike at the top, over a flat elliptical ground shadow.

1) THE SPIKE — the defining must-read — is effectively absent as a sausage. Brown-pixel bounding box is x 208-215, y 105-141: 8 px wide by 37 px tall on a 440 px canvas, i.e. 1:4.6. The stalk beneath it measures exactly 4 px wide (x 209-212, isolated against background from y 142 to ~188). So the 'sausage' is only 4 px fatter than the stem it sits on; a real cattail spike is 8-10x its culm diameter. CORRECTION to the judge: they wrote 'barely wider than a leaf blade' — it is in fact NARROWER than the leaf blades. Isolated single-blade runs measure 13, 16, 13 px at y=185 and 21, 21, 30 px at y=215 (loose-threshold scan gave 19-22 px for the outer blades). The spike at 8 px is under half the width of a typical blade. Second CORRECTION: it is not a smooth 'thread' either — at 20x it resolves as a vertical chain of about nine small tan lozenges with dark gaps between them, reading as a beaded/moniliform seed string, and the colour is a desaturated tan (peak RGB ~90,64,40) rather than the dense dark chocolate-brown velvet of Typha. To read as a cattail this element needs to be roughly 30-40 px wide with smooth unbroken edges and a much darker saturated brown.

2) MALE BRISTLE — the judge is CORRECT and I confirm it pixel by pixel. Rows y=100 through y=103 across x 204-222 are pure background (8,12,18 / 9,13,19); the first non-background pixel in that column is y=104, which is already the top of the brown spike (34,29,25 rising to 90,64,40 at y=105). There is nothing above the spike at all — no thin male flower spike, not even a stub.

3) BARE ROUND STEM — the judge is WRONG here. A bare stem IS visible and IS isolated against the dark background for ~46 px, from y≈142 (immediately under the spike) down to y≈188 where the leaf mass closes over it; scans at y=145/150/155/160/170/180 all return a clean isolated run at x 209-212. The real defect is that this stem is only 4 px wide, is the same flat green as the blades, and carries no round shading or highlight, so it reads as one more hairline blade rather than a round culm. Do not 'add a stem' in the fix — thicken and round-shade the one that exists.

4) LEAF CARRIAGE / ASPECT — the judge is CORRECT and it is quantifiable. Full non-background bbox is x 32-408, y 103-324: 377 wide by 222 tall, w/h = 1.70. The packet specifies aspect 0.35, i.e. nearly 3x taller than wide. The asset is 4.9x wider than spec — and for scale, inside this same family 2.5 is Duckweed (a flat floating carpet) and 2.2 is Water Lily (flat pads on the surface). This Cattail is drawn almost as wide-and-flat as the two species whose whole identity is lying flat on the water. The outer blades on both flanks do not merely reach horizontal: they arch over the top and the tips descend, ending BELOW their own mid-height (leftmost blade y=215 run at x 46-66, rightmost at x 302-355). Nothing in a cattail stand does that. The mustRead 'vertical strap leaves from the base' is not met.

5) EXTRA DEFECT NEITHER PASS NAMED: roughly ten short pale horizontal dashes are scattered through and beyond the foliage (visible as isolated 1-3 px runs at y=150 around x 187-199 and x 241-251, and as free-floating ticks to the upper right of the crown). Several are detached from any blade and float against the background, reading as debris or compression artefacts rather than as leaf highlights.

NET: at thumbnail scale the 8 px tan bead-string disappears entirely and the silhouette is a symmetrical arching fountain of grass — it reads as ornamental fountain grass or a spider plant, not Typha. The single feature that makes a cattail identifiable is missing at usable size, one of three must-reads is wholly absent, and the aspect is out by 5x. FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: three olives or green pea-shaped sweets sitting on a dark serving plate
rows.defect: Duckweed is a carpet of dozens of millimetre-scale discs; this shows exactly THREE huge glossy yellow-green ovals, each large enough to be a lily pad, resting inside a rimmed dish that reads as crockery rather than water. No hair root hangs from any disc — instead a short straight line lies flat ACROSS each oval like a scratch. The scale cue that is the entire point of the species is inverted.
rows.fix: Replace the three big ovals with forty-plus tiny two-and-three-lobed fronds scattered irregularly across the whole width, each dropping one fine hair root downward into darker water, and delete the plate rim entirely.
rows.verifyWhy:
Read at 1:1 and again at 4x/8x/9x zoom on the subject band (source 440x440, subject occupies roughly x=95..350, y=175..250). The FAIL stands, and the organism read is wrong, but two parts of the original claim need correcting before anyone fixes this.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN. (1) A vessel, not a water surface. Under the green shapes sits a cool slate-blue ellipse assembled from four distinct crockery parts: a thin pale-blue RIM RING drawn as a full closed ellipse outline, a dark navy inner BASIN with its own shading gradient, a curved outer WALL that tapers down to a narrow FOOT, and a soft elliptical CAST SHADOW on the ground plane below the foot. That is a plate/saucer read, unambiguously - there is no waterline, no meniscus, no reflected surface, nothing that could be water. Worse, the rim ring is drawn IN FRONT of all three green shapes: at 9x the pale rim line passes straight over the fronds' faces at mid-height, so even taken as crockery the z-order is broken. (2) Three green shapes only, each about 90x50 px on a 440 canvas, i.e. each is ~20% of the frame width. They are not flat films - each carries a strong 3D lens gradient (bright yellow-green top-left falling to olive at the lower-right rim) plus a specular sheen, so they read as solid, thick, glossy beans. Olives on a plate is a fair description of the finished read.

CORRECTION 1 - THE ROOT. The judge said 'a short line lies flat across each one instead'. Half right, but the geometry matters for the fix. Each frond carries ONE short dark-olive segment about 15-20 source px long that STARTS near the frond's own centre and runs RIGHT and slightly DOWN, ending with a small kink and TERMINATING on the frond's own face (on the left frond it dies at the overlap edge). It does not cross the disc, it does not reach either edge, and it does not descend past the frond's lower silhouette. So the must-read 'one fine hair root hanging from each disc' is genuinely absent: what exists is an in-plane stub sitting on the top surface, which reads as a scratch or a cut stem, never as a pendant root in water. The root asset exists in the draw code but is being laid flat instead of hung.

CORRECTION 2 - DO NOT MISTAKE THE RIM FOR A ROOT. There IS a long pale line that runs full-width across all three fronds at mid-height. That is NOT a root and must not be counted as one when re-judging: it is the plate's rim ellipse rendering on top of the fronds. Anyone fixing this by 'shortening the long line across each frond' would be deleting the plate rim and leaving the real defect untouched.

MUST-READS. 'Carpet of tiny oval green discs floating on the surface' - FAILED twice over: count is three, not a carpet, and the scale cue is inverted (three giant beans dominating a dish, when the species is millimetre-scale fronds that should read as dozens of specks skinning a water plane). 'One fine hair root hanging from each disc' - FAILED, see Correction 1. 'No stem, no upright structure at all' - technically satisfied for the plant itself (nothing rises), but the composition adds an entire non-plant upright object (the footed dish) that the reference never calls for and that hijacks the scale read.

FIX DIRECTION: kill the crockery entirely and replace it with a flat water plane (no rim ring, no foot, no cast shadow); multiply the frond count to a dozen-plus small overlapping discs at maybe a fifth of the current diameter; flatten the frond shading so they read as thin films rather than 3D beans; and re-orient the existing root stub to hang DOWN below each disc's lower edge into the water instead of lying on the face.

rows.readsAs: a water lily — a stranger would name the wrong species outright
rows.defect: Every leaf lies FLAT on the surface at water level, which is the one thing the reference explicitly forbids; nothing is held up on a stalk. There is no shower-head seed pod anywhere. The bloom is a small flat six-point pink star lying on the surface, not a large cupped many-petalled bowl. Structurally this is pixel-for-pixel the Water Lily asset with the pads tinted paler and the star tinted pink.
rows.fix: Redraw from a side view: lift two or three big round peltate leaves high above the waterline on tall single stalks meeting each leaf at its CENTRE with the rims curled up like shallow bowls, add a flat-topped green shower-head seed pod on its own stalk, and make the bloom a deep pink multi-layered cup held above the leaves.
rows.verifyWhy: UPHELD, and confirmed by measurement rather than impression. I read the PNG at native 440x440, then re-read it at 4x, at 12x on the bloom, at 10x on a pad, and again through a gamma/gain boost to make sure no faint dark-on-dark structure was hiding above the waterline. WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN: a flat navy ellipse standing for the pond surface, ringed by a thin pale rim line, with a soft cast shadow beneath it; sitting ON that ellipse are three foreshortened green ellipses (pads), all coplanar with the water, all at the same height; a small pink flower with a yellow disc centre sits at pad level near the middle-right, its lower petals OCCLUDED BY the pad in front of it, which proves it is at the surface, not above it. Nothing else exists in the frame. ALL THREE LOTUS MUST-READS ARE ABSENT: (1) 'leaf held high above water on a central stalk, never floating flat' - not merely missing but inverted; the boosted pass shows the topmost subject pixel in the whole image is row 181, which is the top of the pad ellipses and the flower star, so there is no stalk, no raised leaf, no vertical element of any kind. (2) 'shower-head seed pod' - nowhere in the image, at any brightness. (3) 'large pink cupped bloom' - the bloom is a flat radial star roughly 40px across against a 286px subject width (~14%), i.e. small, and it has narrow separated pointed petals around a yellow disc, which is a daisy/star, not a bowl of broad overlapping petals. CORRECTIONS TO THE ORIGINAL CLAIM (verdict stands, two details are off): the bloom has SEVEN narrow petals with a yellow centre disc, not six - the judge miscounted, and omitted the yellow disc, which matters because a yellow disc centre is itself a water-lily cue and is what a fix has to remove; and 'structurally the Water Lily asset retinted' is right but was asserted, not shown - I measured it: Lotus subject bbox is x77-362 / y181-244 (286x64) and Water_Lily's is x71-368 / y181-244 (298x64), identical top and bottom rows, subject-mask IoU 0.90, green-pad-only IoU 0.77; the only real deltas are colour, pad RGB (122,174,150) pale blue-grey vs Water Lily (76,126,85) dark glossy, and flower RGB (240,192,216) pink vs (240,224,240) white. So it is one chassis with two tints, plus about 12px of width. TWO DEFECTS THE ORIGINAL JUDGE DID NOT NAME. First, the pads do not merely lack lotus structure, they actively draw the ANTI-cue: at 10x each pad carries a thin dark wedge line cut from the rim inward toward the centre - that is the water lily's V-notch. A lotus leaf is peltate: the stalk meets the underside at the centre and the blade is an unbroken circle with NO notch, and its rim turns up into a shallow bowl. Both are contradicted here. Second, the packet gives Lotus aspect 0.9 (near square, i.e. tall) and the drawn subject is 286x64, about 4.5:1 wide - it does not just miss its own aspect, it is wider than Water Lily's own 2.2 directive. The single reference cue that is honoured is leafColour: the pads are genuinely paler and blue-grey-green with a waxy read, which is correct for lotus - but colour cannot carry identity when every structural must-read is missing. The packet's explicit note, 'Lotus leaves stand above the water; water lily leaves float on it. Do not conflate,' names precisely the failure that shipped. FIX DIRECTION: this asset needs a different chassis, not a retint - one or two large near-circular peltate blades lifted clear of the water on visible central stalks with upturned rims, a flat-topped shower-head seed pod with sunken seed wells on its own stalk, and a large multi-petalled cupped bowl bloom on a third stalk; the water ellipse can stay as ground, but no leaf may lie flat on it and the notch line must be deleted.

rows.readsAs: a clump of dead or drought-yellowed ornamental grass
rows.defect: The whole identity of papyrus is a tall bare triangular stem with a firework of fine threads bursting from the very TOP — here there is no stem at all and no terminal umbel; the arching parts are thick leaf-blades that leave the ground directly, exactly as in the Cattail and Wild Rice fountains, in khaki. The blades are also far too coarse to read as thread-like rays, and the hatch ticks on them are the same artifact carried over from the shared chassis.
rows.fix: Draw three or four tall naked stems rising two-thirds of the frame height with nothing on them, then explode fifty hair-fine drooping rays radially from each stem tip, with tiny brown spikelets at the ray ends.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD. I read the 440x440 PNG at 1x and then re-cropped and upscaled four regions (base 170,210 110x110 @6x; crown 150,80 150x130 @5x; left tips 20,140 160x110 @5x; whole frame @2x), and also measured the lit-pixel bounding box numerically.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN: a symmetric khaki/olive-gold FOUNTAIN. Roughly 18-22 tapering blades all converge to a SINGLE needle point sitting on the ground shadow at approximately (232,322) and fan outward and over, the outermost pair arching almost horizontal and dipping their tips back down toward the ground at x=22 and x=417. Lit bbox is x[22..417] y[106..321], w=396 h=216, w/h = 1.83. Blade width at mid-length is ~8-10 px on a 440 canvas; tips are blunt rounded caps. There is nothing above the blades at all - the top of the silhouette IS a blade tip.

MUST-READS, ALL THREE MISSING:
1. 'firework explosion of fine drooping threads at the very top' - ABSENT. The crown crop shows only bare blunt blade tips against empty background. No umbel, no radiating point, no spikelets, no harvest structure of any kind. The radiation in this drawing happens at the BOTTOM (ground level), which is the exact inverse of papyrus geometry.
2. 'tall bare three-sided stem with no leaves along it' - ABSENT. There is no stem. Everything leaves the ground point directly.
3. 'clumping from a thick rhizome in water' - ABSENT. All blades issue from one infinitely-fine apex, not a clump of separate culms; there is no water line, no rhizome, no basal brown sheath.

WHERE THE JUDGE'S PROSE NEEDS CORRECTING / SHARPENING (for whoever fixes this):
- 'No tall bare triangular stem' is right but incomplete. There IS one near-vertical member that is taller and straighter than its neighbours - it rises from the base cluster to y~106 (top crop shows it clearly, a single upright reaching well above the fanned blades). It is NOT a stem: it is the same tapering, curving, blunt-tipped leaf blade as the rest, the same width, carrying the same hatch ticks, and it terminates in nothing. But it is the natural anchor for a fix - that member wants to become the culm, be stripped of ticks, given a straight three-sided taper, and given the crown.
- 'It is the Cattail fountain in khaki' is CORRECT and I verified it directly rather than by impression. Cattail.png lit bbox is x[32..408] y[104..324], w=377 h=221 - within a few percent of Papyrus in both extent and vertical registration, same single-point convergence at ground, same outward arch curve, same blunt tips, same free-floating hatch ticks. Papyrus is that generator with a few more blades, a slightly wider spread, no brown spike, and a khaki hue. It is not literally pixel-identical, so do not chase a diff; it is one parametric chassis. Wild_Rice.png (w/h 1.48) is a third, slightly straighter instance of the same fountain, so the chassis problem spans at least three of the seven in this family.
- 'thick arching leaf blades... far too coarse to read as thread-like rays' - CORRECT and understated. At 6x the blades read as sword straps with visible light/dark two-tone shading; nothing in the image is thread-scale.
- 'carrying the same hatch-tick artifact' - CORRECT, and the artifact is worse than a texture flaw. The ticks are short bright horizontal dashes laid across the blades at intervals. Several of them are DETACHED and float in empty background with no blade under them: a cluster around (145..178, 154..160) upper-left and another around (268..288, 158..162) upper-right, both clearly visible in the left-tips and crown crops. They read as debris, not as nodes or ligules.
- One thing the judge did not mention: the COLOUR is also off-spec. The packet asks for 'bright green stem and rays'; the render is desaturated khaki/olive-gold with no green at all, which is why it reads as dead grass.
- Also off-spec: packet aspect is 0.5 (tall and narrow, consistent with the 3-5 m culm). Rendered w/h is 1.83 - roughly 3.7x too wide. The asset is squat where the reference is a column.

VERDICT: the asset reads as a generic clump of ornamental fountain grass / the same object as Cattail-minus-the-spike. Every one of the three must-reads that constitute papyrus identity is absent, plus colour and aspect are wrong. FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a leek, a scallion, or a young aloe — an upright kitchen vegetable, not a seabed meadow
rows.defect: The blades form one narrow closed bundle standing dead vertical and symmetrical: none of the three must-reads survive. There is no lean with the current, no horizontal creeping rhizome with shoots at intervals, and no meadow of parallel straps — it is a single tuft. Three bright green pill-shaped capsules are stuck onto the middle of the blades with no anatomical reading at all; they look like a render artifact pasted over the leaves.
rows.fix: Lay a horizontal rhizome across the bottom of the frame with shoot-fans sprouting at intervals along it, and rake every ribbon blade over to the same side at roughly forty degrees so the whole meadow reads as combed by one current; delete the pill capsules.
rows.verifyWhy: Read the 440x440 PNG, then re-read a 4x nearest-neighbour zoom of the crop (150,80)-(290,350), then measured the green silhouette row-by-row. What is actually on canvas: eight or nine flat mid-green straps with clearly rounded tips, gathered into ONE closed vase/spindle bundle. Measured green bbox x189-257, y109-321 -> 69w x 213h, aspect 0.32 against the packet's spec of 0.70, i.e. it is less than half as wide as specified. Row centreline runs 222.5 at the top to 220.0 at the base - 2.5px of drift over 213px of height - so the thing is dead vertical and bilaterally mirrored: left blades bow left, right blades bow right in matching pairs. Widest point (69px) sits at ~20-30% of the height and it tapers monotonically to a 14px point at y=321. Below y=321 there is nothing but a dark elliptical drop-shadow: no rhizome, no roots, no sand, no substrate, no second shoot. UPHOLDING THE FAIL. All three must-reads are genuinely absent, verified rather than assumed: (1) 'flat ribbon blades all leaning one way with the current' - absent, the 2.5px centreline drift and the mirrored left/right bowing are the opposite of a unidirectional current lean; (2) 'horizontal creeping rhizome with shoots at intervals' - absent, everything converges to a single 14px point of attachment and there is not one horizontal element anywhere in the image; (3) 'meadow of parallel straps rooted in sand' - absent as a meadow. CORRECTIONS to the original claim, which is right in verdict but imprecise in two places. First, the judge wrote 'no meadow of parallel straps' as if the straps themselves were missing - they are not. Parallel flat straps with correctly rounded tips ARE drawn, and there are eight or nine of them; the defect is that they are bound into one closed clump with a single point base instead of being spread across sand as separate shoots, and there is no substrate at all. The blade unit is the one part of this asset worth keeping. Second, 'reads as a leek or scallion' is directionally right but a leek is a straight cylinder; the actual silhouette bulges in the upper third over a pinched base, so it reads closer to a gathered bunch of celery/chard, or an agave/aloe rosette - either way a terrestrial vegetable bundle, not an underwater meadow. The three bright pill capsules are real and the judge described them correctly: at approximately (222,163) a wide horizontal capsule, (222,215) an oval, (222,265) a small circle - all a lighter, more saturated green than the blades, all opaque, all sitting on one vertical centre line and shrinking top to bottom. The top capsule straddles about three blades at once, so it follows no blade edge and has no anatomical reading. Two extra facts the judge did not state and that the fix depends on: the packet specifies harvest 'none visible (inconspicuous flowers hidden inside the leaf sheaths)', so ANY visible capsule is contra-spec here and these should be deleted outright, not repositioned; and their large-to-small descent along a single axis looks like a generic 'nodes at intervals along an axis' routine that was applied to the vertical bundle - it is the rhizome-shoot logic pointed 90 degrees wrong, which is likely the same root cause as the missing horizontal rhizome. Fix direction: lay a horizontal creeping rhizome across the lower third with shoots rising at intervals, give every blade the same one-way current lean, widen to aspect ~0.7 as a spread meadow, and remove the three capsules.

rows.readsAs: a water lily — correct
rows.defect: The read is right: flat pads at surface level with a white star flower sitting among them. But the defining V-notch cut to the pad centre is only a hairline scratch and is essentially invisible at size, so the pads read as plain ovals. The surrounding dark ellipse has a bright pale rim that reads as the lip of a dish rather than open water, and the pads are simple ovals rather than circles seen in perspective. It also shares its exact geometry with the Lotus asset.
rows.fix: Cut a real wedge out of each pad — a visible V opening to the rim, roughly a fifth of the pad's circumference wide — and drop the bright rim highlight so the surround reads as water instead of a plate.

rows.readsAs: a grass clump with a screw or a nail standing in it
rows.defect: The seed head is the identity and it is wrong in both directions: instead of an open airy BRANCHING panicle it is one narrow closed bristle, and it is capped by a solid brown inverted-triangle funnel that reads as a screw head or an arrowhead — a hard geometric shape with no botanical reading, and clearly a broken ornament rather than grain. There is also no sense of the plant standing in water. The leaf spray beneath is the Cattail fountain again in a brighter green.
rows.fix: Replace the bristle and funnel with an open panicle: a central rachis with six to eight fine branches spraying outward and slightly drooping, each hung with separate narrow purple-brown grains, held clear above the leaves.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, and the head description is exact. I zoomed the crown to 12x (orig region x190-235, y92-162 of the 440px canvas). What sits at the top of the plant is: a SOLID brown trapezoidal cap, flat and widest across the top (~16px wide, y98-112), tapering downward to a narrow waist — a countersunk flat-head screw, a funnel, or a lampshade — and beneath it a perfectly straight parallel-sided column ~9px wide and ~40px long (y112-152) built from two vertical rails of small blocky tan grains with a dark slot running down the centre between them. Together they read as a machine screw or a drill bit stuck in the grass, and the dark centre slot makes the screw-thread reading stronger, not weaker. There is NO branching anywhere: no pedicels, no spreading side branches, no drooping lower whorl, no airiness. The whole head assembly is 16px wide on a subject that is 317px wide (5%), where an open wild-rice panicle should be a spreading, airy, roughly-1/3-of-plant-height structure with visible branch orders. Two of the three mustReads are therefore absent outright, and the third is only half-met.

CORRECTION to the judge's second sentence: the leaf spray is NOT the Cattail fountain recoloured. Cattail.png uses broader, sage/olive blades carrying ladder-tick marks along their length and arches much further out (subject W/H 1.70); Wild_Rice uses narrower, more numerous, saturated yellow-green blades with a light-tip-to-dark-base gradient and no tick marks (W/H 1.40); silhouette IoU between them is only 0.45. The real twin is Rice.png in the same folder — it carries the IDENTICAL funnel-cap-plus-grain-column head glyph, only in pale straw instead of brown, over the same blade treatment. So the defect to fix is a shared generic grass-head glyph reused across the whole grass set, not a Cattail copy; wild rice must be differentiated from Rice.png by its panicle, and currently it is differentiated only by hue.

TWO FURTHER DEFECTS the original claim did not mention. (1) ASPECT: the packet specifies aspect 0.5 (twice as tall as wide, 'very tall emergent grass'). Measured subject bbox is x53-369 by y100-326, i.e. 317 wide by 227 tall = W/H 1.40 — nearly three times squatter than spec. The plant reads as a low ornamental clump, not a tall emergent stand. (2) NO WATER: I zoomed the base (x120-320, y280-360). The blades converge into a solid wedge and land on a soft dark elliptical contact shadow — the same dry-ground shadow used by terrestrial flora. There is no water line, no surface reflection, no submerged culm. 'Standing in water' is not depicted at all. Minor: mustRead asks for purple-brown grains; the rendered grains are flat tan/khaki with no purple.

One point in the asset's favour, which is not enough to lift the band: the head IS held clear above the leaf tips (head base y152 vs leaf crest y~155-170), so 'seed head above the leaves' is satisfied positionally. But what is held up there is a screw, not a panicle, so the species reads as generic grass or as Rice.png in brown.

rows.readsAs: a pale-green sago palm or small cycad rosette, or a bristly agave
rows.defect: The identity-bearing must-read is completely absent: there is not one black stem in the image. Every stalk is the same pale apple-green as the blade, and the stalks are not hair-fine wires at all but thick tapering midribs. There are no fan- or wedge-shaped scalloped leaflets anywhere; the leaflets are rendered as tiny stiff triangular sawteeth combed along both edges of a solid lance-shaped blade. The spray is not airy, open or lacy but a dense opaque overlapping shuttlecock-ish mound with almost no background showing through between fronds. The row's own note says drawn with green stalks it is unrecognisable, and that is exactly what shipped. On top of that it is pixel-for-pixel the same drawing as the Sword Fern in this batch, only lighter, so the two most dissimilar ferns in the family are one asset.
rows.fix: Redraw from scratch on a new growth form: fine jet-black glossy wire stems that fork two or three times, spaced far enough apart to leave visible dark background between them, each terminating in a small fan-shaped light apple-green leaflet with a scalloped and notched outer edge, the whole spray broad, flat, open and lacy rather than a solid mound.

rows.readsAs: a dark-green cycad or sago palm mound; a stranger might guess fern but would not commit
rows.defect: The primary must-read, a tight upright shuttlecock crown of long stiff fronds, is not there: the crown is a low spreading mound distinctly wider than tall, with the outer fronds sweeping out horizontally and hooking downward past the base rather than standing up in a vase. The leaflets are not many narrow pointed leaflets running the frond length; they are small triangular sawteeth notched into the edge of a broad solid blade, and the blade centre reads as one continuous paddle rather than a single plane of separate pinnae, which pushes the read toward cycad. No leaflet shows the small forward hook at its base. The rust-brown rows of round sori on the undersides are entirely absent, so the frond backs carry no information at all. The plant also sits low in the frame with dead space above it, wasting the upright format the 1.1 aspect implies.
rows.fix: Rebuild the habit as a tight upright vase: fronds emerging from one basal crown and arcing up and only slightly out so the silhouette is taller than wide, and separate the pinnae into discrete narrow pointed leaflets attached along a thin rachis, each with a small forward-pointing lobe at its base, with a few fronds turned to show rows of round rust-brown sori.

rows.readsAs: a white agave or century plant / a yucca rosette in soil
rows.defect: The leaves are dead-straight rigid spears radiating in a perfect symmetrical fan - no curl, no spidery droop, and no fine furred scale texture; they read as agave blades, not Tillandsia. The identity harvest is completely absent: there is no flattened pink or red bract paddle anywhere, only a bare olive stem carrying a thin lavender bead-spike. And the epiphyte read is inverted - the rosette base plants straight into a ground-shadow ellipse as if rooted in soil, with no bark, branch or wire to cling to.

rows.readsAs: a huge red five-lobed spotted flower - most viewers would land on Rafflesia or at least 'giant corpse flower'
rows.defect: The five russet lobes and pale spotting are there and carry the read, but the central pit is missing - the middle is a convex dark dome, a raised bump rather than a deep cup, and there is no ring of spikes or rim around it. rows.readsAs: a generic lollipop shade tree with a spiky halo and a few brown bugs on it
rows.defect: The broad FLAT-TOPPED crown with tiered horizontal branch plates - the single thing that makes a Cedrus a cedar - is absent; the crown is a plain round green cloud on a bare straight stick. Needles are straight single sticks radiating from the blob centre, never the tight rosette tufts on spur shoots called for. The barrel cones are small screw shapes floating inside and off the side of the foliage rather than standing upright on top of horizontal branch plates, so the 'eggs on a shelf' read is gone. No conifer silhouette at all.
rows.fix: Rebuild the crown as 4-6 stacked flat horizontal branch plates of decreasing width with clear sky gaps between them, and sit the upright barrel cones ON the top edge of the upper plates in silhouette.
rows.verifyWhy:
Verified at 1x and again at 2x/3x/5x/8x gamma-brightened crops (the raw PNG is very dark; brightening is required to see anything on the right half). The FAIL stands, but two parts of the stated cause are wrong and would misdirect the fix.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON THE CANVAS.
TRUNK: a single flat-tan bar of uniform width with hard vertical edges, rounded cap at the bottom, running from the ground shadow straight up into the foliage and simply stopping. No taper, no root flare, no bark texture, no fork, no branch armature of any kind. 'Bare stick' is correct.
CROWN: NOT round — correct this. It is a distinctly BROAD horizontal mass, roughly 300 px wide by 190 px tall in the 440 px frame (~1.6:1 landscape), so the 'broad crown' half of must-read 1 is arguably gestured at. What is absent is everything that makes it Cedrus: the top is a soft lumpy dome of 3-4 blurred bumps, not flat; and there are ZERO tiered horizontal branch plates — no layered shelves, no sky gaps between tiers, no horizontal branch strokes, nothing but one continuous airbrushed green fog with a few darker blotches inside it. The single most load-bearing identity mark of the genus is simply not drawn.
NEEDLES: the judge is right here. ~35 long, straight, single-width pale strokes radiate outward from the crown centre like a pincushion or a dandelion clock. Each is one isolated line; there is no clustering, no spur shoot, no rosette, no whorl. Nothing reads as 'tight rosette tufts'. Several strokes also project well past the green mass into bare background, and two dangle DOWNWARD over the trunk, which no cedar needle does.
CONES: correct this part of the claim. There are FOUR cones and they ARE drawn upright, and they are ridged/segmented barrels — the orientation is right and they are correctly not pendent, so 'rather than standing upright' is a misdescription. Two failures are real but different: (a) nothing supports them. There are no branch tops in the drawing at all, so the two inner cones (approx 172,120 and 228,113 in the 440 frame) sit marooned in the middle of a flat green field with no shelf, no twig, no shading contact — they read as decals floating in fog. The upper-right cone at approx (314,118) is the only one with anything under it, and that is a near-horizontal pale needle stroke, not a branch. (b) The two right-hand cones (approx 314,118 and 322,135) are not strictly outside the silhouette as claimed, but they sit in the thin low-opacity fade zone at the crown's right margin, so they read as unattached and hanging in space. (c) Cone SHAPE is also off: each is widest at the flat top and tapers DOWNWARD to a narrow flat base — a lampshade/inverted cone. A Cedrus cone is a barrel, widest at or below mid-height with a flat or dimpled top.

VERDICT. Must-read 1 (flat-topped tiered plated crown): absent apart from generic breadth. Must-read 2 (rosette needle clusters): absent, replaced by single radiating sticks. Must-read 3 (upright barrel cones on branch tops): half present — orientation and ridging are right, the branch tops they must sit on do not exist. Two of three identity marks missing and the whole silhouette reads as a generic lollipop broadleaf with grass blades stuck in it; it does not even read as a conifer. FAIL upheld.

FIX DIRECTION: build a real branch armature first — a tapering trunk with 4-6 tiers of horizontal branch plates stepping outward, widest at the bottom, cut off flat or slightly domed at the top with visible sky gaps between tiers. Hang the needle mass on those plates as short clustered rosette pom-poms on spur shoots, not as radial single strokes. Then stand the barrel cones ON the upper surface of the top two or three plates so each has a visible shelf line under it, and reshape them so they are widest at mid-height with a flat top.

rows.readsAs: the exact same lollipop conifer-ish tree as Cedar and Redwood
rows.defect: Wrong organism outright. The reference is poison hemlock, a hollow-stemmed umbellifer HERB (form: herb, aspect 0.6), and the render is a tall woody tree - the identical brown trunk, green blob crown and radiating needle sticks used for Cedar and Redwood, decorated with the same brown screw cones. Not one must-read exists: no smooth hollow stem, no purple-red blotching, no finely cut fern-like foliage, no flat white umbrella flower head. A stranger names a pine, not a poisonous weed.
rows.fix: Discard the tree chassis and draw the herb: a slender smooth green stem blotched with purple-red, carrying 2-3 flat white umbels above thrice-cut ferny leaflets.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD. I read the 440x440 PNG at full size and then re-cropped two regions at 3x and 5x nearest-neighbour zoom (stem region x180-270/y210-400; crown region x95-345/y40-240) to hunt for small features before agreeing. Nothing was hiding.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON CANVAS: a single vertical woody trunk, ~14px wide, flat mid-brown (#7a5232-ish) with one slightly darker right-edge shade band and NO other markings, running from a rounded stub cap at y~395 (floating just above a flat black ellipse shadow, not rooted) straight up to y~230 where it forks into two short branchlets that vanish into the foliage. On top sits a single round-to-ovoid green blur cloud (approx x100-345, y45-215) built from soft dark-green airbrush lobes with three brighter mint-green highlight blobs, and roughly 55-70 straight single-stroke green needle lines radiating outward past the cloud edge in all directions, giving a spiky dandelion silhouette. Four brown harvest props hang in the crown at roughly (222,113), (252,120), (302,128) and (208,200): each is an upright ~11x28px cone, broad at the top, tapering to a point at the bottom, banded with 3-4 horizontal ridges so it reads as a screw thread / drill bit.

AGAINST THE REFERENCE ROW (form: herb, aspect 0.6): all three mustReads are absent, not merely faint.
1. 'smooth hollow stem blotched with purple-red spots' - the stem is opaque woody brown with zero purple, red, magenta or mottled pixels anywhere along its 190px length. At 5x the fill is a single flat tone; there is not even a stray speckle to misread as a blotch. It also reads as bark-solid timber, not a hollow green herbaceous stalk.
2. 'very finely cut fern-like leaves' - the foliage is a soft blur cloud plus straight undivided line strokes. Every stroke is a single unbranched segment; there is no pinna, no rachis, no thrice-cut division anywhere. The strokes read specifically as conifer NEEDLES.
3. 'flat white umbrella flower heads' - there is no white anywhere in the image and no flat-topped radiating cluster. The only harvest geometry present is the four brown ridged cones, which is the opposite of the required umbel.
The aspect is also ignored: the row asks for 0.6 (wider than tall, low herb) and the render is a tall narrow lollipop, foliage occupying only the top 40% of frame over a bare 45%-of-height stem.

CHASSIS CHECK (I opened Cedar.png and Redwood.png side by side): the judge is right that this is a shared chassis, with one correction to their wording. It is NOT pixel-identical to both. Hemlock and Redwood are near twins - same trunk width and rounded stub foot, same spiky needle-burst cloud, same four ridged screw cones at the same scale; the only visible difference is Redwood's crown sits ~20px higher and Hemlock's needle strokes are slightly denser. Cedar is the same chassis but visibly differentiated: fatter trunk, larger and much softer foliage cloud with far fewer protruding needle strokes, and only three cones. So the correct statement is: all three are one lollipop-conifer chassis with the crown density and cone count varied, and Hemlock is the variant nearest Redwood. Worth flagging for the family sweep that the chassis fails Redwood's own row too (no buttressed flaring base, no cinnamon fibrous vertical-ridge bark, and the cones are large where the row explicitly warns large cones read wrong).

VERDICT: this is the wrong organism outright. It reads unambiguously as a generic needle-leaved conifer sapling and matches the hemlock CONIFER the note explicitly warns against, not Conium maculatum. No amount of polish reaches the target; the asset needs re-authoring as a low herb: green non-woody smooth stalk with purple-red blotching along it, thrice-pinnate ferny compound foliage, and flat white umbels. FAIL stands.

(Minor extra defects for whoever picks this up: the trunk foot is a rounded stub hovering over a detached shadow ellipse rather than meeting ground; the crown is an airbrushed blur with no leaf-mass structure, so it loses form at the silhouette edge; the harvest props read as screw threads rather than scaled cones even for a conifer.)

rows.readsAs: a bare leafless twig shrub carrying a few bunches of pale berries - an elder or viburnum in winter
rows.defect: The dense prickly evergreen mass that IS a juniper is absent. The render is a sparse fan of about eight bare brown canes, mostly empty background between them, with tiny green tick marks stuck along the canes as a token of foliage; you can see straight through the shrub. No whorls of three, no white stripe on the needles. The blue-grey bloomed berries are the only correct cue, but they are clumped as terminal bunches at the cane tips like an umbel rather than scattered through foliage, and no green unripe ones are mixed in.
rows.fix: Fill the silhouette with overlapping dense blue-green needle sprays until the brown canes are almost hidden, and scatter the bloomed berries singly through that mass alongside green unripe ones.
rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld, with three corrections to the stated causes. What is actually on canvas (440x440, plant occupies roughly x150-300, y85-330): FIVE brown canes -- not about eight -- each about 3px wide, fanning up and outward from a single solid tapered wedge of trunk at the base. The base wedge is the only opaque mass in the whole render: a broom-handle block of flat mid-brown roughly 20px wide that splits into the five canes about a third of the way up. Above that the shape is almost entirely empty background; you can see the black backdrop through every part of the crown. Silhouette is an inverted broom / vase, not a bush and not a column. mustRead 1 (dense prickly bushy or columnar form) is absent -- confirmed.

CORRECTION 1 to the claim: the foliage is NOT 'tiny green tick marks'. Zoomed 8x, the leaf primitive is a set of LONG, straight, unbranched single strokes of dull grey-olive green (about the same length as the gap between two canes, some 40-60px at native scale, i.e. longer than any real juniper needle would read). They cross the canes at wide 30-60 degree angles, many of them floating clear of any cane and passing OVER two or three canes at once so they read as detached sticks rather than attached leaves. This matters for the fix: the defect is a wrong leaf primitive and a wrong attachment model (long lone lines scattered on a wireframe), not merely undersized ticks -- enlarging them would make it worse. It needs dense short needle sprays clothing each cane so the cane wood is mostly hidden.

CORRECTION 2: colour. The strokes are desaturated grey-olive/sage, DARKER than the brown canes and reading as the recessive element. The spec calls for blue-green with silvery bands; there is no blue in the foliage at all, and mustRead 2 (needles in threes flashing a white stripe) is absent on both counts -- no whorl grouping of any kind (each stroke is solitary) and no white/pale band anywhere on a leaf.

CORRECTION 3 / addition the other judge missed: the berries are not just misplaced, they are also the WRONG MIX. Each of the five canes terminates in one tight rosette of 5-7 spheres, about 8px each, pale blue-white with hard white specular dots -- attractive and clearly bloomed, so the 'waxy bloom' half of the harvest note does land. But every single berry is the same ripe pale blue; there are ZERO green unripe berries anywhere, so mustRead 3 ('blue-black bloomed berries mixed with green unripe ones') fails on the mixed-ripeness clause too, not only on placement. Placement claim is confirmed: they sit as terminal bunches perched at the cane tips like umbels, none scattered along the branches or nestled among foliage where juniper cones actually sit.

The judge's read of the overall organism is right: a multi-caned bare-stemmed shrub with terminal umbels of pale berries reads as an elder/viburnum/dogwood in winter leaf-off, not as an evergreen conifer. All three mustReads fail. FAIL stands.

Fix priorities in order: (1) clothe the canes with dense short needle sprays until the wood is 70%+ occluded and the silhouette closes into a solid prickly mass; (2) group needles in threes with a pale/white stripe on the upward face and shift hue to blue-green; (3) redistribute berries along the branch interiors and mix in green unripe ones; (4) break up the solid broom-handle base wedge, which is currently the densest thing in the image and belongs to a different plant.

rows.readsAs: the same lollipop tree as Cedar, slightly greener, with big brown cones
rows.defect: Every must-read is missing. The aspect is specified 0.3 - an extremely tall narrow column - and the render is a wide round crown ball as broad as Cedar's on a short stick, so the defining proportion is inverted. The trunk has no buttressed flaring base and no thick fibrous cinnamon-red bark in vertical ridges; it is the same flat mid-brown untextured taper used across the family. Foliage is radiating single sticks, not flat two-ranked feather sprays. Worst, the reference explicitly warns the cones are olive-sized and that large cones read wrong - the four cones drawn here are enormous, each a good fraction of the crown.
rows.fix: Redraw as a narrow vertical column with a flared buttressed base and ridged red bark, crown no wider than a third of the height, and shrink the cones to barely-visible specks.
rows.verifyWhy:
FAIL upheld, and measured rather than eyeballed. Pixel bbox of the whole tree is 277 x 390 (x 82-358, y 24-413) => aspect 0.71 against a required 0.3. Family context makes it worse: Cedar measures 0.83 and Yew 0.79 at a specified aspect of 1.0, so the Redwood is only 14% narrower than its aspect-1.0 siblings when it should be 3.3x narrower. The single defining must-read, 'extremely tall narrow column', is absent; it reads as the same generic lollipop tree as Cedar and Yew.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. Crown: a soft blobby green cloud spanning the full 277px width and about 210px tall (y 24-233), i.e. WIDER than tall, with roughly 40 straight single-width green line segments radiating outward from a common centre in every direction, sea-urchin / dandelion fashion. There is no branch armature at all, no tiered plates, no drooping leader. Trunk: y 234-413 (180px, 46% of total height), a constant 29px-wide bar.

CORRECTIONS TO THE ORIGINAL CLAIM (three of four points need fixing, the verdict stands):
1. 'Short stick' overstates it. The trunk is 46% of total height, so the proportion failure is not a stubby stem under a ball - it is that the CROWN is as wide as the tree is nearly half as tall. The fix is narrowing the crown and lengthening the column, not just lengthening the trunk.
2. 'The family's flat brown taper' is wrong on the taper. The trunk has NO taper whatsoever: it is exactly 29px wide from y=239 to y=400 and every pixel of it is the single flat value rgb(107,74,46) - zero variation horizontally or vertically, no shading, no ridge lines, no grain, no cinnamon-red hue (it is a mid mud-brown). Cedar, Yew and Juniper sample the identical rgb(107,74,46) at the same relative height, so this is one shared flat-brown trunk primitive across the family. At the very bottom it goes 29 -> 27 -> 21px into a rounded pill cap: the base NARROWS, actively inverting the 'buttressed flaring base' must-read rather than merely omitting it.
3. 'Radiating sticks not flat two-ranked sprays' is exactly right - keep this one verbatim. The needles are unbranched straight strokes from a hub; nothing reads as a flat feather-like spray, and the leafColour 'dark green above with two pale bands beneath' has no counterpart - the green is a uniform mid grass-green blob with no banding.
4. 'Enormous cones' is directionally right but overstated in absolute terms. Blob-measured, the four cones are 13 x 25 px each (at x180/y97, x170/y144, x165/y175, x232/y158) = 6.4% of tree height and 45% of the trunk's width - so ~100x oversized relative to the trunk, which is the error the note warns about, but they are small marks on the canvas, not giant. Shape is also wrong independently of scale: they are elongated ~1:2 horizontally-ribbed screw/beehive cylinders of four stacked bands, not the 'small egg-shaped woody cone about the size of an olive' asked for, and they float unattached inside the foliage cloud with no twig under them.

All three must-reads (tall narrow buttressed column; deep vertical ridged fibrous cinnamon-red bark; flat two-ranked needle sprays) are absent. It does not read as a redwood; it reads as the family's generic round-crown tree chassis with four ribbed pellets stuck in the foliage.

rows.readsAs: a generic round tree with red berries - a rowan, hawthorn or holly
rows.defect: Same trunk-and-blob chassis as Cedar, Hemlock and Redwood with the cones swapped for red fruit. The massive fluted trunk of fused stems with red-brown flaking bark - the thing that makes an ancient yew unmistakable - is a single smooth straight brown stick. The crown is meant to be very dark blackish green and heavy; it is the family's standard mid-green airbrushed cloud, light and airy, with the same radiating needle sticks instead of two-ranked flat sprays. The arils are drawn as tight rosettes of closed round berries, precisely the error the reference calls out - no open-ended red cup with a dark seed showing.
rows.fix: Give it a wide fluted multi-stem trunk with flaking red-brown bark, darken the crown to near-black green with a dense hard edge, and redraw each fruit as an open-topped scarlet cup showing a dark seed.
rows.verifyWhy:
I looked at the full-size PNG and then at 4x-8x crops of the trunk, the crown and two fruit clusters, plus a pixel scan. All three must-reads fail; the FAIL stands, with corrections to the stated causes below.

TRUNK (must-read: 'massive fluted trunk of fused stems with red-brown flaking bark'). Confirmed absent, and worse than the judge described. A pixel scan of the brown region gives width 29-30px at EVERY row from y=260 to y=380 out of a 440px canvas -- perfectly constant, zero taper, zero flare, zero buttress. The fill colour is literally identical at every sample (107,74,46) -- one flat mid warm brown with no value variation at all, so there is no fluting, no fused-stem lobes, no bark ridging, no flaking plates, and not even a light/shadow side. It is not red-brown either; it is a plain saddle brown. It is also the opposite of massive: ~30px of trunk under a ~250px crown, i.e. a lollipop stick, and it terminates in a ROUNDED CAP above the ground shadow instead of flaring into a root buttress. Correction to the judge: they called it 'a single smooth stick', which is right, but understated -- it is a capsule with a rounded bottom end and a single flat fill, so a fix must add taper/flare AND fused vertical lobes AND bark value break-up, not just texture.

CROWN (must-read: 'dense very dark heavy crown'; leafColour 'very dark blackish green'; leaf 'flat soft needles in two ranks'). Confirmed wrong. Centre-of-crown pixels read (52,105,50) and (43,88,42) -- a mid forest green around 30% lightness, nowhere near blackish. The mass is a soft airbrushed blob with three or four lighter lobes; its edge fades out gradually so the background reads through the whole outer third, giving an airy, light, cloud-like crown rather than a heavy dark one. Correction/addition to the judge: the needles are not merely 'airy' -- they are drawn as isolated straight single-pixel-wide dark-green SPIKES radiating outward pincushion/dandelion-style from the crown centre, roughly 40 of them, crossing the silhouette edge. That is the opposite of yew's flat two-ranked sprays and is the specific line-work that has to be replaced (two-ranked feathered sprays lying in planes, dark blackish-green, with the pale underside band showing on down-turned sprays).

ARILS (must-read: 'scarlet open-ended berry-like arils'; note: 'the fruit is an open-topped red cup, not a closed berry'). Confirmed, and this is exactly the called-out error. At 8x each of the four fruit marks is a ROSETTE OF FIVE CLOSED ROUND BERRIES packed in a ring, each berry a full sphere with a bright white specular dot on its upper left and a dark red rim. There is no open top, no cup rim, no dark seed visible anywhere. The five-around-a-centre cluster arrangement plus glossy spheres is a holly/rowan berry umbel, so the judge's 'reads as a rowan or holly' is right; the closed-sphere shading is what sells it. A fix needs single arils, each a scarlet cup viewed from the side or three-quarters with a visible opening and an olive-black seed in it, borne singly along the underside of a spray -- not clustered.

Nothing in the judge's claim was materially wrong. Net: the asset is the family's generic tree chassis (flat brown stick + green blob + radiating spikes) with holly berries pasted on; none of the three yew identity cues is present.

rows.readsAs: a sago palm / cycad, or a generic forked ornamental palm — nobody says 'date palm'
rows.defect: Three things I can see in the render break it. (1) The trunk BRANCHES: the brown pole splits into a clean Y-fork just below the crown, with both arms visible against the background — palms are unbranched, and the fork alone makes this read as the wrong kind of plant. (2) The trunk is a flat, smooth, untextured brown taper from base to fork — there is not one leaf-base diamond, scar, notch or shag on it, so must-read #1 is entirely absent. (3) The date bunches are effectively absent: instead of huge amber-brown bunches on orange stalks hanging BELOW the crown, there is a single pea-sized clump of about a dozen small brown spheres sitting inside the middle of the frond rosette, above the fork — it reads as a coconut cluster or a seed cone, occupies maybe 2% of the crown area, and carries no orange stalk. That harvest mass IS the identity of a date palm. Secondary: the crown is a flat semicircular fan-disc with all fronds radiating in one plane and the lower half of the crown empty, not the open arching shuttlecock described, and the bottom 55% of the frame is bare trunk over empty ground.
rows.fix: Replace the forked trunk with a single unbranched column tiled in overlapping chevron leaf-base diamonds running its full height, and hang two or three fat pendulous bunches of amber-brown dates on visible orange stalks from UNDER the frond bases so they drape clear of the crown against the trunk — each bunch at least as wide as the trunk is thick.

rows.readsAs: an apple tree - correct, but only because the chassis IS an apple tree
rows.defect: The must-read low wide crooked crown on a SHORT trunk is inverted: the trunk is a tall straight untapered stick and the crown is a symmetrical airbrushed ellipse. The fruit are pasted onto the blur with no stalks and no cluster grouping, and there is no hint of the pink-white blossom. Nothing here separates it from Cherry or Jujube except fruit diameter.
rows.fix: Halve the trunk height, flare the base, and fork it into three crooked ascending limbs that carry the crown wide and low, then hang each apple from a visible short stalk off a twig.

rows.readsAs: an orange tree
rows.defect: The broad rounded heart-shaped leaf is genuinely there and is the best leaf decal in the batch, but the reddish leaf stalks are absent, the fruit are flat orange spheres with no velvet bloom, no red blush and no shallow groove, and the trunk/crown are the stock lollipop. The leaf decals sit only on the crown rim so the dense interior is a green blur.
rows.fix: Give each fruit a red-blushed shoulder and a vertical suture groove, and draw the leaves on visible red petioles running into the crown interior rather than only around its edge.

rows.readsAs: an olive tree, or a tree with small black berries
rows.defect: The identity must-read - heavy PEAR-SHAPED fruit - is absent. Every fruit is a small round dark sphere the same size as the apples and cherries, and there is no pebbled skin and no stout stalk. The leaves are small pointed decals rather than large drooping leathery ellipses, and the crown is the standard blur rather than a tall spreading canopy of hanging foliage.
rows.fix: Redraw the fruit as three large pear/avocado silhouettes (narrow neck, heavy bottom) in dark pebbled green, hanging on short stout stalks and sized at least twice the current sphere.

rows.readsAs: a small garden tree with brown berries
rows.defect: The whole identity of this species is architectural and none of it is drawn. There is no immensely tall clean unbranched bole - the trunk is the same stick as Apple's, slightly leaning. There is no flat crown restricted to the very top - the crown is the same rounded ellipse sitting on the stick. The cannonball capsule is rendered as a berry-sized brown sphere with no woody texture and no hole. An emergent rainforest giant is drawn at the same scale and proportion as a hazel.
rows.fix: Give it a 4:1 bare trunk with the crown compressed into a flat plate at the very top, and draw the pods as large heavy woody spheres with a visible pale circular scar at one end.

rows.readsAs: an orange tree
rows.defect: The cashew nut - the single feature that names the species - is completely absent. The fruit are plain round orange spheres with no swollen pear-shaped fleshy apple and nothing hanging beneath them. The reference explicitly warns the grey kidney nut hangs outside and below the fleshy apple; there is no grey shape anywhere in the image. The low wide spreading crown is also not there, it is the stock ellipse on a stick.
rows.fix: Redraw each fruit as a red-yellow pear-shaped cashew apple with a distinct curved grey kidney nut attached to and hanging below its lower tip.

rows.readsAs: an apple tree with slightly smaller apples
rows.defect: The one cluster of three red spheres is the only cherry cue and it is weak - the fruit sit flush against the crown with no long slender stalks and no pairing, so they read as small apples. The shiny red-brown bark with horizontal lenticel bands is entirely missing; the trunk is the same flat brown stick as every other card. No blossom.
rows.fix: Draw the cherries in pairs on long visible thin stems that dangle clear of the foliage mass, and paint the trunk glossy red-brown with horizontal band markings.

rows.readsAs: a small tree with brown berries - identical to the Brazil Nut card
rows.defect: The spiny green burr is the identity and it is absent: the harvest is drawn as three smooth glossy brown spheres, the same asset used on Brazil Nut. No spines, no split burr, no glossy nut inside a husk. The creamy catkin tassels are also absent, and the long sharply saw-toothed lance leaves are drawn as tiny featureless slivers with no teeth.
rows.fix: Replace the smooth brown spheres with green spike-covered burrs, at least one split open to show the brown nuts inside, and add pale drooping catkin tassels through the crown.

rows.readsAs: a palm tree
rows.defect: It is genuinely off-chassis and reads as a palm, but three things are wrong. The trunk FORKS into a second bare limb that dead-ends inside the crown - palms never branch, and that stub reads as a render error. The trunk is plain brown with no grey ringed leaf scars and it stands upright rather than leaning. There is exactly ONE nut where the reference asks for a cluster wedged at the crown base, and the fronds radiate as a stiff one-sided fan rather than arching and drooping outward.
rows.fix: Delete the forked limb and give the palm a single leaning grey trunk banded with horizontal leaf-scar rings, add a cluster of three or four nuts at the frond base, and let the outer fronds arch over and droop below horizontal.

rows.readsAs: a small tree hung with striped melons or gourds
rows.defect: The armour of hard pyramidal spines is the entire identity of a durian and there is not one spike in the image. The fruit are smooth ovals with painted-on vertical stripes, indistinguishable from the fruit on the Jackfruit card. The tall straight trunk with a high open crown is not there either - it is the stock stick and blur, with a few white tick marks on the bark, and the coppery-bronze leaf undersides never show.
rows.fix: Rebuild the fruit silhouette with a jagged spiked outline - the edge itself must be sawtoothed, not a smooth oval with texture - and hang it from a thick stalk on a major branch.

rows.readsAs: a plum or damson tree
rows.defect: The big hand-shaped 3-5 lobed leaf that IS the fig is absent - the crown is built from feathery fern-like fronds with many fine teeth, closer to a rowan or a sumac than a fig. The fruit are small round purple spheres held out on visible stalks, the exact opposite of the reference which requires a pear-shaped fruit sitting directly in the leaf axil with almost no stalk. The smooth pale grey bark is drawn as the usual mid-brown stick.
rows.fix: Replace the frond decal with a large three-to-five-lobed hand-shaped leaf, and seat each pear-shaped fig tight against the branch at a leaf base with no visible stalk.

rows.readsAs: a pear or quince tree
rows.defect: The pale yellow-green round fruit are the right colour and a couple carry a small tip remnant, so it is roughly readable, but the papery calyx crown is barely a nub, the smooth flaking copper-and-green mottled bark is absent (plain brown stick again), and the leaves are alternate-scattered slivers rather than opposite pairs with sunken parallel ribs. The fruit are all bunched at one point low in the crown.
rows.fix: Paint the trunk with mottled copper-and-green flaking patches, and give each fruit a distinct dried five-lobed calyx crown at its tip.

rows.readsAs: a clipped topiary bush with four small onions on wires above it
rows.defect: It escapes the tree chassis but the growth form is wrong in a different way: the foliage is a rigid rectangular slab of near-identical stacked circles with a flat top and straight sides, and the four nuts are stranded ABOVE that silhouette on bare vertical stalks like antennae rather than clustered inside the foliage at branch ends. The multi-stemmed stool is only a tiny brown splay at the very bottom and is almost invisible. The long yellow dangling catkins are absent.
rows.fix: Break the crown into several arching stems radiating from the stool so the outline is a fountain rather than a block, tuck the husked nuts into the foliage in clusters of two or three, and hang yellow catkins from the outer twigs.

rows.readsAs: a small tree with three little striped melons in its canopy
rows.defect: The reference note is explicit that the fruit is cauliflorous and always sits on trunk or main limbs because it is far too heavy for twigs - here the three fruit float up in the middle of the crown, on nothing, exactly where the apples sit on the Apple card. They are also tiny (roughly apple-sized) rather than enormous barrels, and they are the same striped smooth oval asset used for Durian, with no knobbly hexagonal skin. The crown is the standard airbrushed blur, not a dense dark glossy canopy.
rows.fix: Move the fruit down onto the bare trunk, hanging directly off the bark, and scale them up to at least a third of the trunk height with a bumpy knobbly outline.

rows.readsAs: a cherry or crabapple tree
rows.defect: The small dark red oval fruit are about right in colour, but every other must-read is missing: the zigzag thorny twigs that are the giveaway for jujube are nowhere (the crown has no visible twig structure at all), the three strong parallel veins on the small glossy leaves are not drawn, the two-ranked leaf arrangement is not shown, and the fruit are smooth glossy spheres rather than wrinkling date-like ovals. Side by side it is the Cherry card in a slightly darker red.
rows.fix: Draw visible zigzagging twigs with a paired spine at each node carrying the leaves in two flat ranks, and give the fruit an elongated wrinkled date-like body.

rows.readsAs: a generic yellow-fruit orchard tree, close to a crabapple
rows.defect: The fruit are plain round spheres with a highlight dot - no pointed nipple at the tip anywhere, and their colour is a greenish yellow that makes them read the same as the Lime beside them. No thorns at any leaf joint, no purple-flushed buds, and the crown is a dense solid cloud rather than the open straggly one the reference asks for.
rows.fix: Redraw the fruit as an ovoid with a distinct pinched nipple at the lower tip in saturated lemon yellow, and put visible sharp thorns on the exposed twigs.

rows.readsAs: a small citrus tree, but indistinguishable from the Lemon
rows.defect: The four fruit are yellow-olive spheres, not the small round green fruit specified, so nothing separates this from Lemon. No spines in the leaf joints, no winged petiole below any blade, and the foliage is the same matt cloud rather than dark glossy. The fruit are also bunched into two odd pairs instead of clustered among the twigs.
rows.fix: Make the fruit clearly smaller and true green against darker glossy leaves, and draw the winged leaf stalk as a visible second small blade below each main blade.

rows.readsAs: a fern-leaved tree carrying red flower rosettes
rows.defect: The red harvest is drawn as flat pebbled rosettes that sit face-on like flower heads rather than as loose drooping sprays of round fruit, and they are pinned to the crown rim instead of hanging. The crown is a thin sparse blob, not the dense rounded dark crown the reference calls for, and the pinnate leaflets read as bristly fern fronds.
rows.fix: Rebuild the harvest as pendant sprays of three to five separate round bumpy red globes hanging below the foliage, and thicken the crown into a solid dark dome.

rows.readsAs: an orange tree
rows.defect: The fruit are four round orange spheres with highlight dots, identical to the ones on the Orange asset in this same batch - no kidney shape, no long wiry stalk, nothing dangling. The crown is a thin scattered blob rather than a dense dome of drooping lance leaves, so both mustReads are absent and the asset simply duplicates another species in the family.
rows.fix: Draw the fruit as asymmetric kidney ovals in green flushed red-yellow, each swinging on a long visible thread-thin stalk well below the leaf mass.

rows.readsAs: a broad-leaved tree with dark blackberry-like clusters - roughly a mulberry
rows.defect: The berry clusters are the strongest thing in the batch, but they are short stubby clumps rather than elongated knobbly berries, and nothing stains the branch. Every leaf is the same heart shape - the mixed lobed-and-unlobed foliage that is a mustRead never appears - and the broad low spreading crown with crooked branches is once again the family lollipop stick and cloud.
rows.fix: Swap half the leaf decals for irregularly lobed mitten shapes and stretch the berries into longer drooping cylinders with a dark stain smear on the twig behind them.

rows.readsAs: a grey-green narrow-leaved tree with dark fruit - readable as olive
