rows.defect: Identical stamp to flora-h1-s13: same blade count, same V-crotch, same arch curvature, same floating hatch-dashes that do not touch the stems they belong to. Only the hue changed. As a distinct species it is indistinguishable from its blue twin.
rows.fix: Re-seed the arch count, arch spread and blade length from the species seed so the silhouette differs from s13, and attach the leaflets to the blades.

rows.readsAs: a lollipop tree, or a corn dog
rows.defect: The trunk is a flat untapered rounded-rectangle popsicle stick — same width top and bottom, no branching, no root flare — and it drives straight up into the canopy centre like a skewer. The canopy is an out-of-focus green blur with a bald hole punched near its top; the sparse leaf slivers stuck around its edge are the only in-focus geometry, so the crown reads as smoke with confetti in it.
rows.fix: Taper and fork the trunk into two or three visible limbs inside the canopy, and replace the blurred mass with clustered leaf forms so the crown has an edge.

rows.readsAs: a leather flask or a wooden vase with two sprigs of broccoli stuck in the neck
rows.defect: The trunk tapers the wrong way — it is widest at mid-height and NARROWEST where it meets the ground, which no plant does; the silhouette therefore reads as a vessel balanced on a point rather than something rooted. The canopy is only two small teal puffs perched at the upper-left and upper-right, leaving the top of the trunk bare between them.
rows.fix: Invert the taper so the trunk is broadest at the soil with a visible root flare, and close the canopy across the crown so the two puffs read as one foliage mass.

rows.readsAs: a violet fern or cycad — a crown of pinnate fronds
rows.defect: Reads correctly. Notable only that its geometry is the same stamp as flora-h1-s3 down to the curled crozier at the lower-right of the crown; the pinnae are hard flat sawtooth triangles with no thickness.
rows.fix: Vary frond count and spread per seed so it is not s3 in another hue, and soften the pinna tips.

rows.readsAs: a berry shrub — woody stems, pale leaves, red fruit clusters
rows.defect: Reads correctly and is the cleanest structure in the batch: leaves sit on the stems, berries cluster at the tips. The leaves are flat white almonds with no midrib or shading, so the foliage is a little lifeless.
rows.fix: Add a midrib and a light/shadow side to the leaf blade so the foliage reads as tissue rather than paper cut-outs.

rows.readsAs: a yellow-leafed berry shrub — visibly the same bush as s18 recoloured
rows.defect: Same stamp as flora-h1-s18: same fascicle of stems, same four berry clusters at the same tip positions. Worse, the stems here are hard faceted zigzag polylines with sharp elbow kinks that read as bent wire, not wood, and many of the yellow leaf slivers float in the gaps BETWEEN stems without touching any of them.
rows.fix: Smooth the stem polylines into curved woody tapers and attach every leaf to a stem at its petiole.

rows.readsAs: a side table, or a blue lamp with something resting above it
rows.defect: This is not a plant. A hard flat blue ellipse — a disc with no thickness, no leaf edge, no radial structure — sits on a thin brown stick, and a red-and-yellow blob FLOATS ABOVE the disc without touching it, unattached to any stem. Nothing connects to anything. The whole render is heavily blurred so no form has an edge.
rows.fix: Attach the flower to a stem that pierces the leaf disc, give the disc a scalloped rim and radial veins, and drop the blur so the parts read as joined tissue.

rows.readsAs: a green fern or palm clump — pinnate fronds fanning from a crown
rows.defect: Reads correctly. It is however the same stamp as flora-h1-s17, frond for frond including the little curl at the crown's lower right, differing only in hue.
rows.fix: Re-seed frond count, length and fan angle so the green and violet versions do not share a silhouette.

rows.readsAs: a thermometer, a ruler, or a domino standing on end
rows.defect: A pale grey-beige flat slab with a rounded top, perfectly parallel sides, and six evenly spaced horizontal TICK MARKS ruled across it. One tiny cream leaf is stuck to its left flank. Nothing about it reads as living: no taper, no root flare, no branching, no foliage mass, and the regular graduated ticks actively read as a measuring scale.
rows.fix: Replace the ruled ticks with irregular ribbing or areoles, taper the column and flare its base, and add several leaves or spines around the circumference so it reads as a succulent stem.

rows.readsAs: a row of pins stuck in a purple shelf — a broken render
rows.defect: The render is broken. A hard-edged flat purple BAR spans the full frame width at the very bottom, and five tiny white pin-headed stalks poke up from it in two disconnected groups with a wide empty gap between them. The entire top two-thirds of the canvas is empty. Everything is blurred to the point of having no edges. There is no plant body, no stem, no foliage — just a slab and some pinheads jammed against the bottom edge.
rows.fix: Rebuild as an actual organism: replace the purple bar with a rooted basal mass, scale the stalks up to fill the frame, and give the heads real capitula rather than blurred dots.

rows.readsAs: an insect cocoon or a pupa hanging point-down, with three orange buttons on it
rows.defect: The form is an inverted ribbed teardrop that narrows to a point exactly where it touches the ground, so it looks suspended rather than rooted. It has no stem, no leaves and no visible growth direction, and the three orange lozenges stacked up its centreline read as buttons or clasps on a coat, not as botanical structures.
rows.fix: Open the top of the bud into a few emerging leaf tips and widen the base into a rooted foot so it reads as a plant growing upward rather than a pod hanging down.

rows.readsAs: an agave or aloe — a low rosette of thick pointed leaves
rows.defect: Reads correctly and cleanly: leaves radiate from one crown, each carries a visible midrib, the rosette overlaps convincingly. Only quibble is that the silhouette is a near-perfect symmetric half-disc, which makes it feel stamped.
rows.fix: Jitter individual leaf length and tip angle per seed so the rosette outline is not a clean semicircle.

rows.readsAs: a magenta wire mop or a fibre-optic lamp on a stick
rows.defect: Every drooping strand is the same length, the same width end-to-end and terminates in a blunt flat cut at the same height, and each one loops over the crown in an identical hairpin — so the canopy reads as a manufactured curtain of wires, not foliage. There is zero leaf material anywhere on the strands and the trunk is a plain untapered brown dowel with no bark, root flare or taper.
rows.fix: Vary strand length and terminal height by +/-35% and taper each strand to a fine point, then hang small leaf clusters along the lower third of each strand so the curtain reads as vegetation.

rows.readsAs: a green cotton-wool ball on a lollipop stick
rows.defect: The canopy is a single airbrushed blur with no internal leaf clumping or silhouette break — the stray straight spikes poking out of it read as pins stuck in wool rather than fronds. The trunk is a flat brown rounded-rectangle of constant width whose bottom end is a visible rounded cap sitting on top of the shadow instead of entering the ground.
rows.fix: Break the blur into 5-7 overlapping leaf masses with a scalloped outer edge, and taper the trunk outward at the base so it meets the ground plane instead of ending in a rounded stub.

rows.readsAs: a wad of pink candy-floss skewered on a kebab stick
rows.defect: Structural break: the dark stem is drawn straight THROUGH the canopy and emerges above the crown — you can see the stem line crossing the pink mass and continuing past its top edge into empty sky. The canopy is also a single amorphous lump shoved off-centre to the left of the stem with no radial symmetry, no branch armature and no attachment point, so the plant has no growth logic at all.
rows.fix: Terminate the stem inside the canopy mass (draw the canopy after the stem, ending the stem at the crown's lower third) and centre the mass on the stem axis with a short branch fork feeding it.

rows.readsAs: a dark ceramic vase holding two sprigs of lilac
rows.defect: The 'trunk' is a tall tapered vessel — narrow at the base, bulging through the middle, pinching to a neck at the top — with a flat slate fill and a single soft rim highlight down its left side. That is an urn, not a stem: it is roughly 40% of the plant's height in width and reads unmistakably as pottery. The two purple blooms sit at the mouth of it exactly like cut flowers. On top of that the whole asset is so dark it nearly vanishes into the near-black background.
rows.fix: Replace the vessel silhouette with a narrow stem of roughly one-tenth its current width that tapers upward, and lift the value of both the stem and the blooms so the plant separates from the background.

rows.readsAs: a scallop-shell logo or a flat sunburst icon
rows.defect: There is no stem, no trunk and no base of any kind — the whole organism is eleven hard-edged flat-red triangles radiating from a single point that floats above the ground ellipse. Every ray is the same dead flat fill with no gradient, no thickness variation and razor-straight vector edges, and the rays fan sideways and slightly downward so the thing reads as a shell or a corporate sunburst mark rather than anything that grew. It also sits in a completely different rendering language from the painterly assets in this same family.
rows.fix: Give it an actual base — a short thickened stalk or a visible crown of sheathed shoots at the convergence point — and replace the flat triangles with tapered, shaded fronds carrying midrib and edge variation.

rows.readsAs: a cyan wire mop on a stick — the same object as flora-h1-s8 in a different colour
rows.defect: This is a hue swap of flora-h1-s8: identical strand count, identical hairpin loops over the crown, identical uniform strand width, identical blunt terminations all cut to the same height, identical brown dowel trunk and identical ground ellipse. Nothing about the form distinguishes it as a different species, and like its clone it carries no leaf material at all.
rows.fix: Re-seed the strand generator per species — change strand count, droop curvature and terminal height distribution — so this reads as a different plant rather than a recolour of flora-h1-s8.

rows.readsAs: a clump of tall arching grass or sedge
rows.defect: Minor only: every blade converges to a single mathematical point at the base rather than emerging from a crown of separate shoots, and the outermost left blades are so pale and thin they nearly disappear.
rows.fix: Spread the blade origins across a small basal crown 10-15px wide so the clump has a base rather than a vanishing point.

rows.readsAs: a broad-crowned tree with a glowing blue canopy
rows.defect: Best-structured asset in the batch — it is the only one with a real branch armature that forks and thins — but the canopy edge is visibly blocky: hard stair-stepped pixel squares run along the top and left outline and through the bright highlight patches, so the foliage looks like a low-resolution mask scaled up. The canopy masses also float clear of the branch tips, with a visible gap where the branches should disappear into the leaves.
rows.fix: Render the canopy at full resolution with a feathered scalloped edge instead of an upscaled block mask, and overlap the leaf masses down onto the branch tips so the branches enter the foliage.

rows.readsAs: a lumpy purple slug or a deflated balloon lying across the top of a pole
rows.defect: The canopy is a horizontal sausage-shaped slab with knobbly bumps on its upper surface and two flared fins at the left and right ends — it has no radial structure, no thickness at the centre and no relationship to the pole it sits on beyond a few tiny dark fingers underneath. Read as a whole it looks like an animal draped over a post, not foliage or a cap. The trunk beneath is the same featureless straight brown dowel used across the batch.
rows.fix: Give the canopy a domed profile that is thickest over the stem axis and thins toward the rim, and pull a set of visible ribs or branchlets from the trunk out into the underside so the mass is supported.

rows.readsAs: a flat clip-art Christmas tree icon
rows.defect: The entire organism is five stacked isosceles triangles in one dead flat tan fill with razor-straight vector edges and no needle texture, no branch structure, no value change between the lit and shadowed side, and no overlap or irregularity between tiers. The trunk is a hairline dark stick that barely registers, and because the foliage is the same brown-orange as bark the whole thing reads as cardboard rather than a living conifer. It is a flat primitive sitting inside a painterly family.
rows.fix: Replace the flat triangles with layered needle-mass strokes that break the triangle outline into ragged branch tips, and separate the foliage hue and value from the trunk.

rows.readsAs: a cartoon daisy
rows.defect: It reads as a flower without hesitation, but it is pure flat vector: eight identical rounded petals in one uncshaded teal, a solid yellow disc with no floret texture, and a stem that is a constant-width line. The two leaves are rendered in near-white cream rather than any green, so they read as paper cutouts or dead bracts stuck to the stem, and both are identical mirrored lozenges placed at alternating heights with no petiole joining them to the stem.
rows.fix: Shade the petals with a base-to-tip value ramp and vary their length slightly, and recolour the leaves into the plant's foliage green with a visible petiole attaching each to the stem.

rows.readsAs: a violet wire mop on a stick — the third copy of flora-h1-s8
rows.defect: Third hue-clone of the same weeping-strand asset: same strand count, same hairpin crown loops, same uniform blunt strand ends, same straight dowel trunk, same ground ellipse as flora-h1-s8 and flora-h2-s11. The only differences are the strand hue and a slightly greyer trunk. There is still no leaf material on any strand.
rows.fix: Re-seed strand count, droop angle and terminal height per species so the three weepers stop being one asset in three colours.

rows.readsAs: a lumpy purple slug on a pole — the same object as flora-h2-s14
rows.defect: Near-identical twin of flora-h2-s14: the same horizontal sausage slab with the same knobbly upper bumps, the same flared end fins, the same tiny dark fingers underneath and the same straight brown dowel, separated only by a slightly bluer purple. As with its twin the canopy has no dome, no rim taper and no visible support, so it reads as a creature lying across a post rather than a plant crown.
rows.fix: Differentiate the two by re-seeding cap width, bump distribution and droop, and dome the canopy so it is thickest over the stem and thins to the rim.

rows.readsAs: a fountain of golden wheat or sedge
rows.defect: The growth form reads, but the render is dirty: a dozen short yellow horizontal dashes float loose in the middle of the clump, unattached to any blade — they read as stray fragments or a glitch rather than seed heads. The arching blades are drawn as flat gold strokes with a hard black outline and no internal value change, and every blade again converges to one mathematical point at the base with no basal crown.
rows.fix: Anchor the yellow dashes to blade tips as actual seed heads (or remove them) and give the blades a shaded gradient with a spread basal crown.

rows.readsAs: a sheaf of wheat, or a gold paintbrush stood on its bristles
rows.defect: No plant grammar is visible: no leaf, no node, no root flare — the ribs converge to a single needle point that pierces the ground shadow, and the three glowing pods are identical stamped lozenges floating in a channel with no attachment. It is also a straight hue-swap twin of flora-h2-s5.
rows.fix: Flare the base into a splayed root cluster meeting the ground, and vary the rib lengths and pod sizes so the ribs read as separate leaves rather than one extruded fan.

rows.readsAs: a flowering shrub or small blossom tree
rows.defect: The blossom masses are soft airbrushed clouds — the left one in particular has no petal edge at all and reads as a smear rather than a flower head.
rows.fix: Give each blossom cluster three or four resolved petal lobes with a defined outer edge so the crown reads as flowers and not as fog.

rows.readsAs: an artificial tiered Christmas tree, or a stack of dinner plates on a rod
rows.defect: Not an organism. Five hard-edged, perfectly flat ellipses of zero thickness are threaded on a dead-straight brown pole; the discs have no surface texture, no leaf edge, no attachment to the stem, and the pole continues as a bare stub above the topmost disc. Nothing in it is painted — these are flat vector primitives on a dark field.
rows.fix: Replace the flat ellipses with foliage tiers that have thickness, a ragged frond edge and visible attachment to the trunk, and stop the trunk inside the crown.

rows.readsAs: a green wheat sheaf or bundle of scallion stalks
rows.defect: A pixel-for-pixel recolour of flora-h2-s2 — same rib bundle, same crown tips, same needle base, same three pods at the same three heights. On top of that the green is a single flat mid-value with almost no light-to-shadow range, so the ribs read as printed stripes rather than round stalks.
rows.fix: Re-seed the silhouette for this species (different rib count, different crown splay, different pod placement) rather than re-tinting the s2 sheaf.

rows.readsAs: a thorny bramble runner, or a decorated wire
rows.defect: The leaves are single flat needles with one hard white specular streak down each, stamped at even intervals on the shared S-stem; the dark coil-rings alternating along the stem read as loose loops of cord rather than tendrils or nodes. Overall value is so low against the navy background that the whole plant nearly disappears.
rows.fix: Broaden the needles into blades with a midrib and vary their length and angle, and lift the stem value so the silhouette separates from the background.

rows.readsAs: a leafy climbing vine or a vining succulent
rows.defect: Reads correctly as a vine, but the four rosette clusters are the identical stamp repeated at the identical scale and near-identical rotation down the same S-stem used by s6 and s9 — no growth gradient, no smaller young leaves at the tip, no larger ones at the base.
rows.fix: Scale the rosettes down toward the growing tip and rotate each to its own angle so the vine reads as grown rather than beaded.

rows.readsAs: a teal plastic Christmas tree with a stray purple lens flare
rows.defect: The same five flat zero-thickness ellipses on the same straight pole as flora-h2-s4, recoloured teal. In addition a magenta glow sits behind the stem between the top two tiers with nothing generating it — it reads as a render artifact, not as a feature of the organism.
rows.fix: Give the tiers real frond geometry and thickness, and either remove the unexplained magenta bloom or anchor it to a visible emissive structure on the stem.

rows.readsAs: a cluster of golden eggs or metal pods on a wire
rows.defect: The appendages are smooth featureless ovoids with faint radial seams and no midrib, stem attachment or leaf tip, so they read as fruit or eggs rather than foliage; they are also large enough to bury the shared S-stem, which survives only as a thin thread glimpsed between them.
rows.fix: Give the ovoids a leaf tip and midrib and shrink them so the stem stays continuously readable through the cluster.

rows.readsAs: a grey boulder in a dust cloud
rows.defect: Nothing that identifies a fungus is present — no cap, no stipe, no gills, no pore surface, no colony structure. It is one lumpy grey mound with a flat interior and a scatter of white dots hovering around it, and it reads unambiguously as a rock.
rows.fix: Give it fungal identity: a domed cap edge with a lip, a visible underside, and clustered fruiting bodies rather than a single undifferentiated mound.

rows.readsAs: a sea urchin, or a spiny fruit cut in half
rows.defect: The two spiny spheres have real volume and the sectioned face with its internal web is genuinely interesting, but nothing narrows it to a fungus rather than an urchin or a seed pod. The wide brown elliptical wash behind the pair is a stray background glow with no source and floats free of the ground shadow.
rows.fix: Add a short basal attachment and a spore-mass texture to the cut face, and replace the loose brown halo with a grounded contact shadow.

rows.readsAs: nothing — an almost empty dark tile
rows.defect: The render is effectively invisible. There is no silhouette, no edge, no ground shadow — only a faint bluish haze in the centre of the frame and a scatter of dim grey dots. Held at arm's length the tile is blank; no viewer could name any organism from it.
rows.fix: Raise the body value and restore a defined silhouette edge so the form separates from the background at all.

rows.readsAs: a purple rock, or a mound of violet dust
rows.defect: The identical mound outline and speckle field as fungi-h0-s0, recoloured purple. As with s0 every fungal must-read is absent — no cap edge, no stipe, no gills, no fruiting bodies — and the interior is a single flat wash with the specks sitting on top of it like noise.
rows.fix: Break the mound into a cluster of distinct capped fruiting bodies with visible undersides so it reads as fungus rather than as a tinted copy of s0.

rows.readsAs: a mushroom
rows.defect: The cap-and-stipe silhouette is right, but the cap is nearly the same near-black navy as the background so the top half of the organism barely separates from the field; the cap texture is a flat repeating lattice wallpaper rather than painted surface; and the stipe is a straight tapered slab with no base flare, volva or mycelium where it meets the ground.
rows.fix: Lift the cap value well clear of the background and flare the stipe base into the ground shadow.

rows.readsAs: a puffball — or, just as readily, an egg or a pearl
rows.defect: Good volume and lighting, but it is a perfectly smooth sphere: no basal attachment, no skin texture, no pore or rupture, and the grey specks read as dirt on a shell rather than as spore pitting. The perfect circle plus the sharp cast shadow pushes the read toward egg.
rows.fix: Break the perfect circle with a slightly irregular outline and add a basal attachment plus a spore-pore or apical split at the crown.

rows.readsAs: a morel or inky-cap mushroom - the only asset here a stranger names as a mushroom
rows.defect: The cap is genuinely modeled and lit, but the stipe is a flat cream slab with zero shading, zero taper and no base - a paper cutout glued under a rendered cap - and the cap's bottom edge is a hard horizontal cut with no veil, gill line or junction where the two meet. The surface pattern is a regular diamond lattice that repeats without following the cap's curvature, so it reads as printed upholstery rather than a morel's pitted ridges.
rows.fix: Shade the stipe with the same light as the cap, taper it and widen it into a base, and warp the lattice along the cap's UV so the cells compress toward the silhouette edges.

rows.readsAs: two blue stones or eggs, one sliced open
rows.defect: The cut-away sibling is the one real fungal idea in the batch - a sectioned puffball showing gleba - but the cut face is a flat plate filled with a thin white scribble of unclosed lines that reads as cracked ice, not as chambered interior tissue. Both bodies float on a large brown vignette ellipse with no cast shadow and no point of contact, so they hover. The little dark spikes on the outer body are 2-3px flat triangles that read as compression noise rather than warts.
rows.fix: Give the cut face real depth - an inner wall, a darker gleba mass and a paler rind band - and land both bodies on a shadow so they sit on the substrate instead of hovering.

rows.readsAs: two purple party balloons
rows.defect: Two perfectly smooth gradient spheres with a scatter of dark freckles and nothing else. No ostiole or apical pore, no warted or scurfy skin, no sterile base, no mycelial grip on the ground - every cue that separates a puffball from a ball is absent, and the pure vertical gradient plus the crisp rim highlight is exactly balloon rendering. The two spheres intersect but do not merge, leaving a hard seam where they overlap.
rows.fix: Add the identity cue - a puckered apical pore on the larger body and a pinched, wrinkled sterile base gripping the soil - and break the smooth gradient with a warted skin texture.

rows.readsAs: a naval contact mine, or a cartoon virus icon
rows.defect: A sphere with six long straight spikes radiating from it and a single dark dot dead center. The dot sits where an eye would sit and immediately reads as a face, pushing the whole thing into the animal/creature register. The spikes are flat unshaded triangles lying entirely in the picture plane - none angles toward or away from the viewer, none is foreshortened, and they are drawn in a flat mid-tone with no light on them at all, so they look pasted onto the rendered ball rather than growing out of it. Nothing in the image says fungus: no substrate, no stipe, no hymenium, no mycelium.
rows.fix: Drop the centered dot, and rebuild the spikes as shaded three-dimensional cones distributed over the whole hemisphere with foreshortening, so they read as a spiny earthstar/spore body rather than a mine.

rows.readsAs: a teal plastic bowl and a smaller matching bowl
rows.defect: The bright cyan rim outline drawn around a hollow dark interior is bowl rendering, not fungal rendering. The interior is a single smeared dark radial gradient with no hymenial surface, no depth and no floor. The only fungal signal is the fringe of grey bristles under the rim, and those are rendered as thin desaturated grey hairs that read as dust or noise against the saturated teal body rather than as teeth or a lacerate margin. Neither body shows any attachment to a substrate.
rows.fix: Line the cup interior with a visible hymenium - a distinct inner wall with its own shading and a concave floor - and recolor the marginal bristles into the body's own hue family so they read as tissue rather than dirt.

rows.readsAs: a windswept flat-topped tree, or a coral
rows.defect: The best-drawn asset here, but it is one of three indistinguishable copies (s2, s8, s19) - same six trunks, same splay, same drooping outrigger arms, same flat-bottomed dome canopy, same twig fringe, separated only by a hair of hue. Standing alone it also reads as vegetation rather than fungus: the multiple straight vertical trunks rising from bare ground into a horizontal canopy is tree grammar, and the branch tips are so finely subdivided they blur into a leaf mass.
rows.fix: Differentiate this instance structurally from s2 and s8 - change trunk count, branching angle and canopy profile per seed - and thicken and fuse the lower trunks into a single fleshy basal mass so it reads as one coral-fungus fruiting body rather than a grove.

rows.readsAs: the same windswept flat-topped tree as s8 and s19
rows.defect: Visually indistinguishable from fungi-h0-s8 and fungi-h0-s19 - I compared them side by side and could not find a structural difference anywhere: identical trunk count and spacing, identical branch topology, identical canopy silhouette and identical drooping side arms. Only a faint warm-vs-cool white shift separates them. As with its twins, the straight trunks under a flat canopy read as a tree, not a fruiting body.
rows.fix: Drive trunk count, branch angle, canopy width and asymmetry from the species seed so no two coral-form species share a silhouette.

rows.readsAs: a small bunch of dark grapes hanging from a stick
rows.defect: Barely visible at all - the fruiting body is a dark blue-grey against a near-black field, at a contrast so low that on a normal screen the asset is mostly empty frame. What does resolve is four overlapping glossy spheres with elliptical specular hotspots, which is grape/berry rendering; the spheres never boolean together, so you can see the buried circle outlines cutting through the front surfaces. The brown substrate bar hovers in mid-air with a hard black smear beneath it and no connection to any ground, and the cluster hangs off its underside with no visible attachment point.
rows.fix: Raise the fruiting body's value far above the background, merge the spheres into one continuous surface, and attach the cluster to the branch with a visible base rather than letting it dangle.

rows.readsAs: an orange, or a small desert planet
rows.defect: A single smooth orange sphere with a scatter of dark freckles, floating above an elliptical shadow. There is not one fungal feature in the frame - no stipe, no cap, no pore, no substrate, no mycelium, no second body, no texture. The freckle scatter plus the warm gradient plus the crescent rim light on the right edge is literally planet shading, and at this hue a stranger says 'orange' before anything else. This is the base sphere primitive shipped as a species.
rows.fix: Give it an identity: pinch a sterile base into the soil, add an apical pore and a warted or areolate rind so it reads as a puffball rather than fruit.

rows.readsAs: a wad of chewed bubble gum stuck under a twig
rows.defect: Same chassis as s3 - the identical floating brown arc with an identical three-sphere cluster slung beneath it, hue-swapped to yellow. The yellow at least gestures at a slime mould, but the spheres are unmerged: you can clearly see the outlines of the rear circles printed through the front ones, plus stacked lens-flare highlights on each. The substrate bar again floats with no ground contact, and the mass hangs from it with no attachment or wetting where the two touch.
rows.fix: Fuse the blobs into one metaball surface with a single coherent highlight, and flatten and spread the mass where it meets the branch so it appears to be creeping over the bark.

rows.readsAs: six spent matchsticks stuck in a pad, or bean sprouts
rows.defect: The pin-mould idea is legible and this is one of the better structural reads, but the execution is flat: the six stalks are dead-straight lines of constant width with no taper, no curve and no shading, and two of them cross in a hard X that no stalk growing from a common pad would make. The sporangia are dark ovoid beans with a hard white specular each, reading as coffee beans rather than spore heads. The brown substrate pad is a plain ellipse with a few short vertical tick marks and reads as a shadow the stalks are standing in.
rows.fix: Taper and gently curve each stalk so it bends under its own head, uncross the crossing pair, and translate the sporangia into darker, matte, slightly translucent heads instead of glossy beans.

rows.readsAs: two jellyfish
rows.defect: Two smooth red domes with a dense curtain of long thin filaments hanging from their rims - that is medusa anatomy, bell plus tentacles, and it is what a stranger names instantly. It is made worse by the geometry: the filaments pass straight THROUGH the brown substrate bar and continue well below it, dangling into empty space, so the spines are not resting on or growing over the substrate at all, they are drifting past it. The domes themselves are featureless gradient hemispheres with a thin dark line at the rim and no cap texture, no stipe, and no attachment to the bar they are supposedly fruiting from.
rows.fix: Stop the teeth at the substrate line and shorten them to roughly a third of the cap depth so they read as a hydnoid hymenium, and attach each cap to the branch with a visible lateral stipe or a broad fused base.

rows.readsAs: the same windswept flat-topped tree as s2 and s19
rows.defect: The third copy of the coral-fan chassis. Placed beside s2 and s19 I cannot tell them apart - same six trunks from the same origin, same outrigger arms drooping to the same height, same canopy dome, same twig density. Three species share one picture. Independently it also reads as a tree rather than a fungus because of the straight vertical trunks and the horizontal leaf-like canopy.
rows.fix: Seed-drive the branching parameters (trunk count, split angle, canopy aspect, asymmetry) so each coral species gets its own silhouette, and fuse the trunk bases into one fleshy stem.

rows.readsAs: a clump of teal grass or a small aloe
rows.defect: Ten upright blades rising from a dark base. The problem is that each blade is a flat leaf with a lighter crease running up its center - a midrib - and a broad flattened body narrowing to a fine point, which is plant leaf grammar; a club or spindle fungus is a rounded, swollen, unribbed column. Several blades also lean and overlap like grass rather than standing as separate fruiting bodies, and the base is a flat black smear with no clump, no mycelial mat and no soil, so the whole cluster appears cut off rather than emerging.
rows.fix: Remove the midrib crease and give each blade a rounded, waxy cross-section that swells toward the middle before tapering, and add a pale fused clump at the base where they emerge from the substrate.

rows.readsAs: a dark conical mushroom on a pale stalk
rows.defect: Reads correctly as a mushroom, but the cap is a single flat near-black shape carrying a 2D diamond-lattice wallpaper that ignores the cap's curvature entirely — no terminator, no rim shading, so the cap reads as a printed decal rather than a volume; no gills, annulus or veil remnant anywhere.
rows.fix: Shade the cap as a solid of revolution (light the upper-left shoulder, darken the lower rim) and warp the lattice along the cap's UV so the diamonds compress toward the silhouette edge.

rows.readsAs: a naval mine or a cartoon virus particle
rows.defect: The sphere plus single dark apical pore does give a puffball read, but the eight spikes are flat in-plane triangles pasted only at the silhouette edge — none sit on the front of the ball, so they read as a starburst decal behind a smooth egg rather than as spines growing off a spore sac. The body surface is perfectly smooth with no warts or scurf.
rows.fix: Scatter the spines over the whole visible hemisphere with foreshortened, tapering bases that shade into the body, and drop the count of long equatorial spikes.

rows.readsAs: two empty ceramic bowls with a brush glued under the rim
rows.defect: The cup-fungus read is only half there: the interiors are smooth featureless gradients with no hymenial texture, the rims are hard-edged polygons, and the black bristle fringe hangs under the rim as a stiff comb of identical straight hairs that reads as a scrubbing brush or eyelashes, not as hairs on an apothecium. Neither cup shows any attachment to a substrate — they float on one shared shadow.
rows.fix: Curl and vary the marginal hairs so they sweep outward with random length, and add a granular/pitted hymenium plus a visible basal attachment point to the ground.

rows.readsAs: a green naval mine
rows.defect: Pixel-for-pixel the same spiked sphere as fungi-h1-s1 and fungi-h1-s18 with only the hue changed — same eight edge-only triangular spikes, same single centred dark dot, same shadow ellipse. Nothing about the form distinguishes this species from its two siblings.
rows.fix: Vary the chassis per seed — change spine density, body ovality and pore size — instead of tinting one shared sphere.

rows.readsAs: two lumps of blue clay, one warty and one cracked
rows.defect: Closest thing in the batch to a puffball pair, but the two bodies are inconsistent with each other: the left is covered in tiny raised spikes while the right carries thin white scribbled cracks that read as scratches rather than areolate splitting. Neither has a sterile base, stem or ground contact, and the backing is a huge brown elliptical glow far larger than the ground shadow used on every other asset in the batch.
rows.fix: Give both bodies the same surface ornament family at two ages (young warty, old splitting) and replace the oversized brown glow with the standard tight ground shadow.

rows.readsAs: a clump of purple grass or small aloe leaves
rows.defect: These are flattened blades with a central midrib highlight, a leaf-like taper to a point and one blade curling over at the tip — that is plant foliage, not a fungus. Club and coral fungi are round in section, blunt or lobed at the tip and fleshy at the base; none of that is present. A stranger names this a plant every time.
rows.fix: Rebuild the fingers as round-sectioned clubs that swell toward blunt, slightly lobed tips and fuse into a common fleshy base, and delete the midrib highlight that is creating the leaf read.

rows.readsAs: a dark conical mushroom on a pale stalk
rows.defect: Correct mushroom read, but it is the same master as fungi-h1-s0 with a marginally taller stipe — same cap outline, same flat unlit diamond lattice, same cream stipe, same shadow. As a distinct species it adds nothing, and the cap again shows no form shading at all.
rows.fix: Differentiate this seed from fungi-h1-s0 with a real morphological change (bell vs conical cap, flaring or bulbous stipe base) and light the cap as a volume.

rows.readsAs: a moon or asteroid
rows.defect: A single smooth grey-blue sphere with scattered dark pits and a thin white crescent arc of rim light on the upper right — that is a planetary body, and the pits read as impact craters. There is no fungal must-read on it at all: no pore, no stipe, no ornament, no mycelial base, no ground contact beyond a detached drop shadow.
rows.fix: Give it an apical pore and a rooted sterile base, replace the crater pits with raised warts or scurfy scales, and kill the crescent rim light that is producing the planet read.

rows.readsAs: two halved kiwi fruits or orange bowls
rows.defect: The identical cup pair from fungi-h1-s10 with the hue swung to orange; in this colour the smooth glossy interior and the dark hairy fringe read as fruit halves rather than fungi. Same defects carry over: featureless hymenium, hard polygon rim, comb-straight marginal hairs, no substrate attachment.
rows.fix: Break the shared chassis — different cup depth, eccentric rim and a stalked base for this seed — and texture the disc so it does not read as fruit flesh.

rows.readsAs: a toothed/hedgehog fungus fruiting on a log
rows.defect: The strongest asset in the batch — two caps with a dense curtain of hanging spines on a woody substrate reads correctly as Hericium/Hydnum. Weaknesses: the caps are perfectly smooth featureless half-domes with a hard blue-grey line along the top edge, the teeth are uniform straight strands that hang well past the log and start to read as tentacles, and the log itself is an undifferentiated brown lozenge with no bark or end grain.
rows.fix: Taper and vary the teeth so they shorten toward the cap margin, and give the log bark texture plus a cut end so the substrate reads as wood.

rows.readsAs: a red naval mine
rows.defect: Third recolour of the same spiked sphere (see fungi-h1-s1 and fungi-h1-s11): identical eight edge-only flat triangular spikes, identical central dot, identical body silhouette and shadow. The spikes still lie entirely in the picture plane so the object reads as a 2D sun-burst behind a ball.
rows.fix: Distribute spines in 3D over the hemisphere and vary spine length/count per seed so the three siblings stop being one object in three colours.

rows.readsAs: a grey rock, or a cloud of dust
rows.defect: A flat low-poly grey wedge with no volume shading, sitting inside a haze of loose white speckles that spill well outside its outline. Nothing on it is fungal — no cap, stipe, pore, gill, hypha or substrate — and the shape has no top/bottom orientation, so it reads as a boulder or a debris cloud. The stray speckles floating free of the silhouette also read as a render artifact.
rows.fix: Replace the flat polygon with a shaded crust or resupinate patch that visibly clings to a substrate, and bind the speckle particles to the body surface instead of scattering them into the background.

rows.readsAs: a white broadleaf tree, or a bleached coral head
rows.defect: The branching is a tree generator: hair-fine terminal twigs of uniform width packed into a smooth flat-topped canopy dome sitting on a bundle of bare trunks. Coral fungi branch dichotomously into thick fleshy tips, not into a foliage-density fractal, so the fungal read loses to 'tree' for any stranger. There is also no mycelial or leaf-litter base — the trunks just meet a shadow ellipse.
rows.fix: Cut the recursion depth by half and swell the branch tips into blunt fleshy clubs so the mass reads as coral fungus rather than as a canopy.

rows.readsAs: red coral, or a bundle of bare twigs
rows.defect: Same branch generator as fungi-h1-s2 at lower density. The branches are constant-width tubes with hard rounded ends and no taper from base to tip, and the four vertical stems are near-identical parallel rods, so the whole thing reads as plastic rod stock rather than fleshy tissue. The dark outline stroke around every branch flattens it further.
rows.fix: Taper every branch from a thick base to a fine tip, splay the basal stems outward from a shared fused foot, and drop the uniform dark outline.

rows.readsAs: a small cratered moon or an ice planetoid
rows.defect: A single smooth pale-blue sphere with a soft rim highlight and scattered dark pits, floating over a cast ellipse. Nothing fungal is present — no stipe, no cap, no gills or pores, no substrate, no mycelium. The dark speckles read as impact craters, and the vertical gradient reads as planetary terminator lighting, so the object names itself as a celestial body.
rows.fix: Seat it on a substrate and give it a fungal surface: split the sphere into a rounded cap with a visible in-rolled margin over a short stipe, and replace the crater dots with a peeling warty veil texture so it reads as a puffball rather than a moon.

rows.readsAs: a naval contact mine, or a virus icon
rows.defect: A teal ball with eight straight, rigid, needle-sharp lances radiating at even angles, plus one dark dot dead centre that reads as a pupil or a detonator port. The spikes are hard geometric triangles with no taper variation and no organic base swelling, and the whole thing floats free of any substrate. It is the same ball as h1-s6 with the hue changed.
rows.fix: Kill the radial-lance primitive entirely and rebuild as a spined earthstar — a dome sitting in a split leathery basal star, with short soft conical warts that thicken at the base instead of even needles.

rows.readsAs: the same naval mine in cream instead of teal
rows.defect: Pixel-for-pixel the same construction as h1-s5 — identical ball, identical eight straight lances at the same angles and lengths, identical centre dot, identical ground ellipse — with only the fill recoloured from teal to bone white. It reads as a mine or a sea-urchin toy, not a fungus, and its existence alongside h1-s5 makes the recolour obvious in a side-by-side.
rows.fix: Give it a genuinely different body plan from h1-s5 rather than a palette swap — e.g. an open funnel/chanterelle with a wavy decurrent margin — so the two seeds do not resolve to the same silhouette.

rows.readsAs: a broken render — a yellow brain-blob with a detached brown bar hovering above it
rows.defect: Render defect, not just a read problem. A long dark-brown shallow arc spans almost the entire frame width, floating in empty space well ABOVE the yellow lobed body and never touching it — the substrate log has come unstuck from the organism it is supposed to support and is stranded in the sky. The yellow body itself has no ground shadow of its own, so it also floats. The lobed blob is the only readable part and on its own is a passable witch's-butter, but the composition is broken.
rows.fix: Re-anchor the substrate: place the log behind and BELOW the fruiting body so the lobes visibly erupt from its bark, and clip the log to the frame instead of letting it run edge to edge.

rows.readsAs: a clump of purple grass or a small aloe
rows.defect: A fan of hard-edged, straight-sided straps that taper to sharp points and sit on a flat cut-off baseline. The edges are ruler-straight and the shading is a flat vertical gradient, which gives leaf-blade stiffness rather than the soft, slightly translucent, irregularly forking clubs of a coral fungus. It also shares its entire construction with h2-s14 (same count, same lean, same foot line), just recoloured.
rows.fix: Fork the upper third of each strap into two or three uneven fingers with blunt rounded tips and let the bases merge into a shared pale mycelial foot, so it reads Clavaria rather than grass.

rows.readsAs: two grey boulders, or a contact-binary asteroid
rows.defect: Two overlapping matte slate-grey spheres with a thin bright rim arc on the upper left of each and a pepper of dark pits across both. Identical primitive to h1-s4, just doubled and desaturated. There is no cap, no stipe, no margin, no attachment to anything; the pits read as cratering and the rim light reads as a sun terminator. A stranger names rock, not fungus.
rows.fix: Make it a bolete pair — swell each ball into a bun-shaped cap with a visible pale pore underside and a thick tapering stem, and set both stems into a litter base.

rows.readsAs: a dragon-blood or banyan tree in silhouette
rows.defect: Beautifully rendered and internally coherent, but it names a woody TREE, not a fungus: thin arching trunks rise from a common base and split into a dense twig-crown with a flat-topped canopy dome. Nothing here is fungal. It is also the first of three near-identical copies (h2-s10, h2-s13) that differ only in tint and a couple of degrees of crown width, so the family reads as one tree repeated.
rows.fix: If this generator is meant to be fungal, replace the twig-crown with a fused bracket shelf and thicken the trunks into a single stout stipe; otherwise reserve it for the flora family and give the fungi seeds a cap-and-stipe generator.

rows.readsAs: a mushroom — a morel or shaggy-cap
the same banyan tree, in cool grey
rows.defect: A direct repeat of h2-s0 — same fan of thin arching trunks from one point, same trunk count, same flat-topped lobed crown, same tiny speck cluster floating in the trunk gap — with only a slight hue shift toward grey and a marginally wider crown. It reads as a tree rather than a fungus, and read next to h2-s0 and h2-s13 it reads as the SAME tree three times.
rows.fix: Drive real structural variation off the seed — trunk count, crown asymmetry, whether the canopy is a shelf or a globe — instead of tinting one canopy.

rows.readsAs: a blue nebula smudge or a smear of glowing paint
rows.defect: A soft-edged amorphous blue mass with granular dots and a diffuse outer bloom. It is readable as a plasmodial slime mould, so it is not the wrong kingdom, but it has no structure at all: no advancing fan front, no vein network, no substrate contact, and no ground shadow — it floats in the middle of the frame. It is also the same blob as h2-s15 with the hue changed, including the same notch on the upper right of the outline.
rows.fix: Give it a directional plasmodium: a fan-shaped advancing margin at one edge feeding back into branching yellow-veined strands, and let it drape over a visible log or leaf so it has something to creep on.

rows.readsAs: two glowing jellyfish sitting on a floating log
rows.defect: Two smooth teal domes trail long, thin, evenly spaced, brightly glowing strands well below their rims — the strands read as jellyfish tentacles, not as the crowded soft spines of a toothed fungus, because they are separated, uniform in length and lit from within. The brown substrate bar behind them is again detached: its left end floats clear of the ground ellipse and it passes BEHIND the domes rather than being the thing they erupt from.
rows.fix: Crowd and shorten the spines into a dense continuous fringe hanging directly from the cap underside, drop the internal glow, and seat the caps ON the log with a visible attachment scar.

rows.readsAs: the banyan tree again, third copy
rows.defect: The third instance of the h2-s0 / h2-s10 tree with no structural change — identical arching trunk fan, identical flat-topped twig canopy, identical speck cluster between the trunks. It names a tree, not a fungus, and its presence makes the repetition undeniable when the three are viewed together.
rows.fix: Retire two of the three: let this seed produce a distinct fungal form (e.g. a tiered polypore stack on a stump) rather than a third tint of the same canopy.

rows.readsAs: a tuft of dry amber grass, or stylised flames
rows.defect: The h1-s8 blade cluster recoloured to orange — same straight-sided tapering straps, same sharp tips, same flat baseline, same count and lean. The warm gradient pushes it further toward a flame motif. No fungal cue is present: no forking, no blunt clubbed tips, no mycelial mat.
rows.fix: Differentiate it from h1-s8 structurally, not chromatically — make these fused, flattened, antler-like branches (a stagshorn) with blunt bifurcated tips.

rows.readsAs: a violet nebula smudge
rows.defect: The h2-s11 blob recoloured purple — same lumpy outline with the same notch at upper right, same granular speckle, same diffuse halo, same absence of a ground shadow so it floats. Passable as a slime mould only by default; it has no margin, no veins, no substrate, and nothing that distinguishes it from its blue twin beyond hue.
rows.fix: Give this seed a fruiting stage instead of a plasmodial one — a field of tiny stalked sporangia on hair-thin stems rising off a dark crust — so it cannot be confused with h2-s11.

rows.readsAs: a wet brown boulder, or a raw potato, dusted with gold glitter
rows.defect: There is no fungus anywhere in the picture — no cap, no stipe, no gills, no substrate. It is a single flat amorphous polygon with a soft airbrush gradient and randomly scattered orange dots, floating with no ground contact. It is the same silhouette as fungi-h2-s5 and microbe-h0-s1 in a different hue.
rows.fix: Replace the lump with an actual fruiting body: a distinct stipe rising from a mycelial base into a domed cap with a visible cap/stipe junction and a shaded gilled underside.

rows.readsAs: a bunch of green grapes, or soap bubbles, hanging under a stick
rows.defect: The growth form (a cluster attached under a branch) is fungally plausible, but the rendering kills it: six perfect glossy translucent spheres with hard specular highlights read as balloons/fruit, not flesh. The spheres merely touch the branch rather than fusing into it — no attachment tissue, no stem, no shared base — so the cluster looks hung on rather than grown from. Identical geometry to fungi-h2-s19.
rows.fix: Fuse the spheres into a lobed shared mass with a visible attachment collar on the branch, and kill the glass specular in favour of a matte, slightly rough flesh surface.

rows.readsAs: three bare winter saplings in purple, not a coral fungus
rows.defect: The coral-fungus intent is legible in the tufted branching outline, but every branch is a uniform-width hairline that forks at hard woody elbows and droops at the tips like twigs; coral fungi taper upward from thick fleshy stipes into blunt fingertips. The three stipes are also cleanly separated cylinders with hard highlight stripes, reading as three plants rather than one clump. Same geometry as fungi-h2-s8.
rows.fix: Taper the branch widths from thick at the fork to blunt rounded tips, remove the downward-drooping twigs, and merge the three stipes into one fused fleshy base.

rows.readsAs: a cluster of teal bubbles or grapes under a branch
rows.defect: Pixel-identical layout to fungi-h2-s17 with the hue rotated — same branch arc at the same height, same sphere count and stacking, same highlight placement. Individually it is only a colour variant, and the spheres again read as blown glass rather than fungal flesh; the elongated white highlight ovals sit on top of the forms like decals.
rows.fix: Reseed this one's cluster geometry (different lobe count, sizes and hang angle) and give the caps a matte, faintly wrinkled surface instead of the glass highlight.

rows.readsAs: burnt matchsticks stuck in a patch of dirt
rows.defect: The stalked-sporangium read is nearly there, but the stalks are perfectly straight hairlines of constant width with no taper or curve, and the heads are grey ovoids carrying two crescent white highlights each that read as eyeballs. The soil ellipse is a flat brown oval with hard stroke marks and the stalks visibly pass through it rather than emerging from it. The whole assembly sits small and high in the frame with a large dead margin all round.
rows.fix: Taper and gently curve the stalks, seat them into a textured substrate instead of over it, and replace the double crescent highlight on the heads with a single soft sheen.

rows.readsAs: a child's drawing of the sun, or a sea urchin
rows.defect: A plain yellow radial-gradient circle with about eight straight triangular spikes poking out of it and one small grey dot dead centre. Nothing fungal is present — no stipe, no cap edge, no substrate connection; the ball hovers above a detached black shadow ellipse. The single centred dot reads as an eye and pushes it further towards a face/creature read. It also occupies only a small part of the frame.
rows.fix: Ground it as an earthstar or spiny puffball — sit the sphere on a split leathery basal star, replace the straight spikes with dense short conical warts across the whole surface, and remove the centre dot.

rows.readsAs: five long teal leaves, or canoes, stuck out of a wooden post
rows.defect: The bracket-fungus must-read is absent: instead of semicircular fans with concentric zonation and a pored underside, each shelf is a lanceolate blade that comes to a sharp point, with a midrib-like interior arc — literally a leaf. A black hairline runs along each blade's top edge and overshoots past the tip into empty space, a stray stroke. The trunk is a flat untextured brown rectangle with hard vertical edges, clipped off both the top and the bottom of the frame. Identical geometry to fungi-h2-s7 and s9.
rows.fix: Redraw the shelves as blunt half-moon fans wider than they are deep, with banded concentric growth zones and a shaded underside, and give the trunk bark texture and a visible top or base inside the frame.

rows.readsAs: a mossy green rock, or a blob of algae
rows.defect: Same amorphous lump as fungi-h2-s16 with the hue changed to green — same wide low polygon, same soft glow halo, same scattered speckles. No cap, no stipe, no gills, no substrate, no ground contact. Nothing identifies it as a fungus or as any organism at all.
rows.fix: Give it a real fruiting structure — stipe, cap and gilled underside — or if it is meant to be a crust/slime fungus, drape it over a visible log so the growth habit is readable.

rows.readsAs: a clump of teal grass or an aloe rosette
rows.defect: Seven flat, sharply pointed blades rising from a common base — the silhouette is grass, not a fungus. Clavarioid fungi are rounded club-shaped fingers, blunt at the tip and swelling toward the middle; these are knife-edged and taper to a needle point, and each carries a hard bright edge highlight that reads as a leaf's specular. The base is a dark ellipse the blades sit on rather than emerge from.
rows.fix: Round the blades into blunt-tipped clubs of varying thickness, remove the knife-edge highlight, and let them emerge from a pale mycelial base rather than a shadow ellipse.

rows.readsAs: four pink leaves, or petals, jammed into a wooden post
rows.defect: The same trunk-and-blade template as fungi-h2-s4 recoloured pink: identical flat rectangle trunk clipped top and bottom, identical pointed lanceolate blades at the same attachment heights, identical interior arc and identical black hairline overshooting each tip. The shelf form that would make it a bracket fungus — a blunt fan with zoned banding and a pored face — is absent, so it reads as foliage.
rows.fix: Reseed the shelf geometry away from s4 (different count, depth and droop) and redraw each shelf as a blunt semicircular fan with concentric bands and a visible pored underside.

rows.readsAs: three leafless orange saplings, a winter shrub
rows.defect: Colour-swapped twin of fungi-h2-s18 — same three stipes from the same shadow ellipse, same hairline twig lattice, same drooping side branches. The branches never thicken toward the base and fork at hard angular elbows, which is woody tree grammar rather than the soft upward-tapering fingers of a coral fungus; the tips end in sharp points instead of blunt swollen ends.
rows.fix: Give the branches real taper (thick at the base, blunt at the tip), curve the forks instead of elbowing them, and reseed the branch pattern so it does not mirror s18.

rows.readsAs: four salmon fillets nailed to a fence post
rows.defect: Third recolour of the same trunk-and-blade template as s4 and s7, and in this orange-red hue the pointed blades with their pale interior arc read unmistakably as raw fish fillets. Same defects carried through: no fan shape, no zonation, no pored underside, a black hairline that runs off past each tip into empty space, and a flat untextured trunk rectangle clipped at both the top and bottom edges of the frame.
rows.fix: Redraw as true brackets — blunt half-moon fans with banded growth zones and a shadowed pored underside stepping down the trunk — and texture the trunk so it reads as bark.

rows.readsAs: a blue bacterial colony under a microscope, or a nebula
rows.defect: The read is broadly right — a glowing colony with scattered rod-shaped cells and darker inclusion granules. But the underlying blob is the same amorphous polygon as the fungi lumps and its hard grey outline is visible cutting across the glow at the top and lower left, which betrays the shared chassis. Several dark blue hairline strokes hang off the right side, curling out past the colony edge and clipping at the frame border, reading as stray marks rather than flagella. The rods are all one length and one width, scattered at uniform density with no clumping or division pairs.
rows.fix: Hide or dissolve the polygon outline into the glow, pull the stray right-edge strokes back inside the frame and attach them to cells, and vary rod length with a few dividing pairs.

rows.readsAs: almost nothing — a barely-visible dark grey smudge on a black field
rows.defect: The render is effectively broken by contrast: the cell body is a near-black grey almost identical in value to the background, visible only as a faint outline, and the four internal organelle circles are only marginally lighter. At a glance the tile looks empty. Underneath it is again the shared amorphous polygon, here with a sharp pointed spur jutting off the right side that reads as a snag in the outline rather than a structure. No membrane definition, no cytoplasm texture, no flagellum or cilia.
rows.fix: Raise the body value hard against the background (or add a rim light) so the cell is legible at a glance, and give it a defined membrane plus one motility structure.

rows.readsAs: nothing — a faint smudge on black; you have to hunt for it
rows.defect: The blob is painted at roughly the same value as the background plate. The lobed outline, the three circular vacuoles and the nucleus are all present but sit only a few percent above black, so at portrait size the frame reads as empty. This is a legibility break, not a weak read — its clone s17 proves the chassis is fine when it is actually lit.
rows.fix: Lift the body value and add a rim-light on the membrane so the silhouette clears the background by at least 30% luminance, as s17 does.

rows.readsAs: four potatoes or asteroids in a curl, sitting on a firework starburst
rows.defect: The radiating hairlines are a separate flat starburst layer: every line converges on a point down-left of the sphere cluster, so they pass behind the body instead of emerging perpendicular from the cell wall — they read as motion rays, not cilia. The largest sphere carries a dark elliptical pit that reads as an impact crater, pushing the whole cluster toward asteroid. Body is four smooth gradient balls with no membrane material.
rows.fix: Re-root the cilia on the membrane outline itself, normal to the local curve and tapering, and replace the crater ellipse with an organelle that sits under the surface rather than punched into it.

rows.readsAs: a glass jar or bottle a third full of green liquid
rows.defect: A perfectly straight horizontal chord cuts the lower third of the ovoid with darker green beneath it — the unmistakable read of a liquid meniscus in a container, reinforced by the hard opaque white circle stuck on the upper-left like a glass highlight decal and a tiny white bead sitting on the right end of the line. There is no cell structure of any kind: no nucleus, no organelle, no membrane texture, no motility feature. It reads as a vessel, not a living thing.
rows.fix: Delete the straight fill-line and replace the interior with a nucleus plus cytoplasmic granularity that follows the ovoid's curvature; break the highlight into a soft anisotropic sheen instead of a hard disc.

rows.readsAs: a curl of cream-coloured eggs or potatoes on a starburst
rows.defect: Same asset as s11 with the hue swapped to bone-white — same off-body starburst convergence point, same crater ellipse on the lead sphere, same speckle dots. Nothing about the form, arrangement, spike count or crater placement is re-rolled by the seed, so as the second sample of this chassis it adds no species information at all.
rows.fix: Let the seed drive form as well as hue — vary the chain length, the curl direction and the cilia rooting — and fix the starburst to originate on the membrane.

rows.readsAs: a badminton racket, or a comb laid inside an oval
rows.defect: Entirely flat line-art: a thin white ellipse outline, a rank of straight vertical comb teeth hanging from a central axis, and a horizontal barbell with three round nodes on it. There is no body mass, no interior fill, no depth or shading anywhere — it violates the painterly-canvas standard and reads as a technical diagram or a sports implement. Nothing in it says organism.
rows.fix: Give the ellipse an actual painted body with volume and a lit membrane, then convert the comb teeth into ciliary rows that attach to and deform that body rather than floating inside an empty outline.

rows.readsAs: a pollen grain or a virus capsid — a scaled spore ball
rows.defect: Reads correctly and has real volume: the scale lumps break the silhouette so the sphere is knobby rather than a pasted circle, and the rim light sells the curvature. Only note is that it is the same chassis as s2 with hue swapped.
rows.fix: Vary scale size and packing density per seed so s2 and s15 stop being the same ball twice.

rows.readsAs: three sausages, or three two-tone chopsticks stacked on a shelf
rows.defect: The frame holds three separate near-identical rods lying in parallel, each running almost the full width of the canvas, each with a bead-like sphere at its midpoint joint and hatch marks on one half only. They are not connected to each other and no one of them is a body — so there is no single organism in the portrait, just a repeated prop tiled three times. The glossy two-tone plastic shading pushes it further toward sausage than cell.
rows.fix: Commit to ONE organism — either fuse the rods into a single articulated filament with a visible cell wall, or reduce to one rod and build the portrait around it at proper scale.

rows.readsAs: an amoeba or a single cell — roughly right, but murky
rows.defect: The read is correct but dim: the rust body sits low against the near-black plate and the only crisp edge is a thin outline stroke. The three vacuole circles are barely separated in value from the cytoplasm, and the membrane outline breaks near the right edge where a small tab of the contour juts out of the silhouette. Interior is a flat radial gradient with no cytoplasmic material.
rows.fix: Raise interior contrast between cytoplasm, vacuoles and nucleus, and close the broken contour on the right edge.

rows.readsAs: a purple nebula, or a bruise-coloured stain smeared on a slide
rows.defect: There is no organism and no silhouette — just a soft-edged rectangular haze filling the frame corner to corner, dusted with scattered short rods and a few grey circles. Because the mass has no boundary the portrait has no subject. Three or four curved appendage lines hang off the RIGHT edge, unattached to any body and cut by the frame, which reads as stranded debris.
rows.fix: Give it a bounded colony body with a readable outer margin inside the frame, and root the curved flagella on that margin so they are not clipped floaters.

rows.readsAs: spilled pharmaceutical capsules — pills or tic-tacs
rows.defect: A scatter of a dozen bone-white capsules, all the same width, most the same length, a few crossed at random. The bacillus reading is available but the capsule shading is glossy pharmaceutical rather than cellular, there is no cell-wall texture, no dividing septa, and no size or stain variation, so the pill read wins. As a portrait it also lacks a focal subject — every rod has equal weight.
rows.fix: Add cell-wall grain, varied rod lengths and a couple of mid-division septa, and pull one rod forward as the focal cell.

rows.readsAs: a spore or pollen grain — a glowing scaled cyst
rows.defect: Correct read with genuine volume; the teal internal glow between scales gives it a living translucency the rest of the batch lacks. Only note is that it is s15's sphere with a hue change.
rows.fix: Re-roll scale count and packing per seed so this and s15 are not the same ball.

rows.readsAs: a gold nebula or a spark shower — a stain, not a creature
rows.defect: Identical construction to s18 in amber: a full-bleed soft haze with no boundary anywhere, so there is no subject in the frame. Rods and grey dots scatter over it without organising into a body. The long curved filaments on the right run into and are cut by the right frame edge, stranding them outside any organism.
rows.fix: Bound the colony mass well inside the frame with a readable margin and attach the filaments to it instead of letting them exit the canvas.

rows.readsAs: a tardigrade / water bear — named instantly and unprompted
rows.defect: Identity is unmistakable: plump barrel body, eight stubby ventral legs with visible claw prongs, blunt snout with eye dot and mouth. Weaknesses are finish rather than identity — the four segment lines are straight strokes that ignore the barrel's curvature and stop short of the edge, and the surface is a smooth plastic gradient with no cuticle texture.
rows.fix: Curve the segment lines around the body and carry them to the silhouette, and add cuticle grain to kill the plastic sheen.

rows.readsAs: a tardigrade / water bear
rows.defect: Same correct read as s4 — and same asset: identical topline, identical leg placement and claw shapes, identical head and mouth disc, identical straight segment lines, identical cast shadow, with only the hue moved from orange to green. Correct as an organism, but it carries zero new species information next to s4.
rows.fix: Drive leg spacing, body proportion and cuticle pattern from the seed so the two water bears are visibly different animals, not one repaint.

rows.readsAs: a glass marble or a spirit-level bubble half full of green liquid
rows.defect: A single olive sphere with a hard grey rim ring, one big specular dot and a PERFECTLY STRAIGHT horizontal green fill edge cutting the lower third — a rect clipped to a circle, not a biological boundary. No membrane, no organelle, no cilia, nothing that reads as alive; it sits small and lonely in the middle of the frame.
rows.fix: Replace the straight fill line with an irregular painted cytoplasm mass inset from the wall, add a nucleus and a granular membrane edge so the sphere reads as a cell rather than a bead of glass.

rows.readsAs: streptococcus — chains of blue cocci
rows.defect: Reads correctly. The three chains float with no medium, and every coccus is the same flat matte blue with no wall texture or division furrow, so it is legible but plain.
rows.fix: Vary coccus diameter slightly along each chain and add a faint division furrow where two cells meet.

rows.readsAs: a ciliated cell cluster, but at first glance a lens-flare starburst
rows.defect: The cilia are dead-straight, perfectly evenly spaced rays radiating from a single point, and they are drawn DARKER than the near-black background — they read as scratches or a starburst filter, not as beating cilia. The one dark groove on the big sphere is the only feature. Geometrically identical to microbe-h1-s1 (same spheres, same rays, tan hue).
rows.fix: Curve the cilia, break their spacing and phase, anchor them to the membrane rather than to a common centre, and light them brighter than the ground so they read as appendages.

rows.readsAs: segmented spirilla / filamentous rods with a nucleus bead
rows.defect: Reads as a microbe. The bottom rod carries a dark unlit duplicate of itself running off to the right, which reads as a stray ghost rather than a rod lying behind.
rows.fix: Light the rear rods at a dimmer value of the SAME hue rather than as near-black silhouettes so they read as depth.

rows.readsAs: a bundle of orange segmented rods with nucleus beads
rows.defect: Correct read, but it is the microbe-h0-s9 die with one more rod and the hue rotated teal to orange; the four dark brown ghost rods behind muddy the middle of the frame.
rows.fix: Give this seed a different segment pitch and rod taper from h0-s9 so the two are not the same organism in two colours.

rows.readsAs: a tan ciliated cluster, again reading as a starburst artifact
rows.defect: A pure recolour: sphere positions, the dark oral groove and every radial ray match microbe-h0-s8 exactly, only tan instead of mint. The rays are again straight, evenly fanned and drawn darker than the background, so the cilia are nearly invisible and read as scratches.
rows.fix: Re-seed the cluster arrangement (different sphere count and curl) and re-draw the cilia as curved, brighter, membrane-anchored filaments.

rows.readsAs: flagellated protists — Euglena-like cells with an eyespot
rows.defect: Best asset in the batch: teardrop bodies, a red eyespot, a long whipping flagellum on each. The four cells all point the same way with near-identical body shapes.
rows.fix: Vary body length and flagellum phase between the four so they read as a swarm rather than four stamps of one cell.

rows.readsAs: a wireframe diagram — a stadium plan or a CAD ellipse, not an organism
rows.defect: The body is EMPTY: a thin orange outline ellipse with no fill, no shading and no volume, filled with a comb of straight radial hairs and one horizontal axis line dotted at both ends and at centre. It is line art, not a painted organism, and violates the no-flat-primitive rule outright.
rows.fix: Fill the ellipse with a shaded cytoplasm body and lit membrane, and convert the axis line and hair comb into internal structure read through a translucent wall.

rows.readsAs: a green glass marble
rows.defect: The h0-s6 die recoloured green: same grey rim ring, same specular dot at 10 o'clock, same three white specks, same dead-straight horizontal fill edge across the lower third. Nothing in it reads as a cell — no nucleus, no membrane grain, no appendage.
rows.fix: Give the sphere an irregular inset cytoplasm mass, a visible nucleus and a granular wall, and drop the glassy rim ring that makes it read as glass.

rows.readsAs: a white wireframe oval — a diagram or a badminton shuttle grid
rows.defect: Identical geometry to microbe-h1-s11 in white: hollow unfilled outline ellipse, straight radial hair comb, one dotted horizontal axis. No body, no shading, no volume — the render is a line drawing and the identity is absent.
rows.fix: Paint a filled shaded body under the outline and re-seed the geometry so it is not h1-s11 in another colour.

rows.readsAs: a branching chain of blue cocci — streptococcus
rows.defect: Correct read and the chain walk differs from h0-s7, but it is the same die in the SAME blue, so as a distinct species it is indistinguishable from h0-s7 at thumbnail size.
rows.fix: Shift hue or coccus size distribution so this seed is not confusable with microbe-h0-s7.

rows.readsAs: a green marble or a soap bubble
rows.defect: The third stamp of the same sphere die (h0-s6, h1-s12): grey rim ring, one specular dot, white specks, and the same straight horizontal fill boundary cutting the lower third. Slightly ovoid this time, but still no organelle, no membrane texture and no appendage — it does not read as a living cell.
rows.fix: Replace the clipped-rect fill with painted cytoplasm and add at least one organelle plus a textured wall.

rows.readsAs: scattered rod bacteria — but closer to spilled gel capsules
rows.defect: Eight teal lozenges of near-identical length and thickness scattered across the frame with one faint dividing line each. They have no wall texture, no flagella and no polarity, so they read as pills; the top three sit in a row as a vertical-dash-vertical arrangement that reads as typography rather than a colony.
rows.fix: Vary rod length and curvature, add a division furrow and a wall grain, and cluster them into a colony rather than an even scatter.

rows.readsAs: a magenta nebula or a smeared gram stain, not a single organism
rows.defect: The render is clipped: the magenta mass runs off the right edge of the canvas and several straight filaments are cut clean by the frame border, with the cloud also touching top and bottom. What is inside is an unresolved blur of soft blobs, tiny pink dashes and flat grey circles with no membrane, no outline and no coherent body — there is no organism to name, only a fog.
rows.fix: Shrink and centre the colony so nothing touches the frame, and resolve a bounded body with a readable membrane instead of an edge-to-edge blur.

rows.readsAs: streptococcus — two chains of cocci, one straight run of seven and one hooked chain
rows.defect: Beads are perfectly uniform in radius and each carries the identical ten-o'clock highlight, so the chain reads slightly like strung pearls; no capsule, no division septum, no texture.
rows.fix: Jitter bead radius +/-15% and vary the overlap so a couple of cocci read as mid-division diplo pairs.

rows.readsAs: spirochetes — magenta corkscrew bacteria with whip flagella
rows.defect: The coils are crowded into a single arc across the top third and overlap into a tangle, and every helix uses the same amplitude and wavelength so it reads as one spring copied four times.
rows.fix: Vary pitch and amplitude per cell and spread them across the frame so at least one corkscrew is isolated and legible on its own.

rows.readsAs: a glass marble or snow globe half-filled with green liquid — not an organism
rows.defect: A rimmed slate-blue sphere with a hard outline, a white specular blob at ten o'clock, three speck-bubbles and a dead-flat horizontal chord across the lower third filled solid green. The flat liquid line is a container cue; there is no membrane texture, no nucleus, no organelle, no cilium, no flagellum, nothing biological anywhere in the shape. It is the same drawing as s7, s8 and h2-s0 with the hue swapped.
rows.fix: Delete the flat fluid chord and the glass specular entirely; replace with an irregular deformable membrane outline plus an offset nucleus and two or three internal vacuoles so it reads as a protist cell.

rows.readsAs: a tardigrade (water bear)
rows.defect: Only one eye spot reads and the head lobe sits as a separate ball fused onto the body; no mouth stylet or terminal claw detail on the rear pair.
rows.fix: Cut a small round terminal mouth into the head lobe and give the hindmost leg pair visible claws so the water-bear read is unambiguous.

rows.readsAs: chained cocci, but arranged into an arrow or lambda glyph
rows.defect: Three bead-chains meet at a single junction point, producing a hard three-way branch and an overall arrow/rune silhouette. Cocci chains do not fork at a shared node; the composition reads as a typographic mark rather than a smear of bacteria. Same bead primitive and same uniform radius as s18.
rows.fix: Break the three-way junction — let the chains cross over each other with depth separation instead of sharing one bead.

rows.readsAs: a clump of tan spheres inside a sunburst — the halo reads as a graphic starburst, not as pili
rows.defect: The corona is drawn in a value DARKER than the background field, so the radiating lines read as scratches or a comic-book impact burst; they are also perfectly straight, evenly spaced and radially centred, which no fringe of pili or cilia is. The front sphere carries a large dark oval that reads as a hole or damage rather than a pore.
rows.fix: Repaint the corona lighter than the background with per-hair length and curvature jitter so it reads as a flexible pilus fringe instead of a sunburst.

rows.readsAs: three purple ladder-rung strips — zip ties or diatom filaments
rows.defect: Three near-identical horizontal bars stacked with even vertical spacing, each spanning nearly the full frame width and each carrying an unexplained sphere bead at its midpoint. The repetition and even spacing read as a diagram or a chart, and the mid-bar bead has no biological reading — it looks like a bolt through a strap.
rows.fix: Vary the three filaments in length, angle and rung spacing and drop or justify the mid-bar bead (make it a heterocyst with different colour and outline) so they read as living filaments.

rows.readsAs: an olive glass ball with liquid in the bottom
rows.defect: Identical geometry to s2, s8 and h2-s0 — rimmed sphere, ten-o'clock specular blob, speck-bubbles, flat horizontal chord with darker green fill — only the hue changed to olive. Here the fill is shallower and a stray white streak sits on the fluid surface, reinforcing the liquid-in-glass read. No cell structure of any kind is drawn.
rows.fix: Replace the whole primitive with a genuine cell: irregular membrane, offset nucleus, and a visible flagellum or cilia band breaking the outline.

rows.readsAs: a green glass marble half full of darker green liquid
rows.defect: The third instance of the same chassis in this batch alone. Rimmed sphere, one white specular blob top-left, tiny bubble specks, dead-flat horizontal fluid line across the lower third. Nothing distinguishes it from s2 and h2-s0 except saturation, and the identity read is a container, not an organism.
rows.fix: Kill the flat chord and the glass rim; give the cell a deformed pseudopod outline and internal granulation so it reads as an amoeboid protist.

rows.readsAs: spirochetes — coral corkscrew bacteria with fine flagella
rows.defect: Same coil generator as s19 with only the hue changed, and the helices are dark-cored so the ribbon reads slightly flat against the background.
rows.fix: Differentiate this species from s19 with a distinct coil pitch and cell length, and lift the ribbon's core value so the helix separates from the field.

rows.readsAs: a green snow globe or a marble with liquid settled in the bottom
rows.defect: The fourth copy of the same sphere-plus-flat-fluid-line chassis, differing from s8 only by being stretched into a slight oval. Same hard rim, same ten-o'clock specular blob, same white speck-bubbles, same dead-flat horizontal fill line. No membrane, nucleus, organelle or motility structure is present, so nothing in the image names a microbe.
